speechtext: I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce has the chairman of the grain commission working on that now. I will direct his attention my hon. friend's question.

Public works, salaries, $689,655.

["The first three bills, Nos. 17, 18 and' 19 appear on the order paper as being printed in both languages. As to the other two, Nos. 20 and 21, I am informed by the Clerk that they are now printed in both languages and an indication to that effect was made on the sheet which I have."]

When this item was under consideration the other day a discussion arose which I think was of very much greater importance than, perhaps, the majority of the members of the House realized. It touched upon a very vital matter in connection with not only this department but several other departments. An analysis was being secured from the minister of -the amounts annually paid to retired civil servants of his particular department, and there was difficulty in ascertaining out of what -particular fund it was paid, or under what heading. The minister gave us a figure which was somewhat startling, that in the year 1924 $75,600 had been paid out for superannuated or retired servants of has department. I made a search through the estimates to find out how this was disposed of. This was in the Public Works department, of course, and I located it under " Superannuation," I will refer to that in a moment. The minister shows an apparent saving this year in salaries of some $18,000 or $19,000, but when we take into consideration the huge amount that is being paid out to civil servants in his department on being retired under the Calder Act and under the Superannuation Act, we find that as a matter of fact the cost of this department, in common with other departments, has actually increased by a very large sum. In other words, while there have been retirements brought about during the past few years, it seems that the places of those who have retired have been filled immediately and the full strength of the staff maintained. If hon. members will turn to -page 25 of the Estimates they will see revealed in striking and very accurate figures the enormous extent to which this annual retirement allowance has grown. Under " Superannuation " there is ian item entitled "Statutory" which reads as follows:
Civil Service Superannuation and Retirement
Act, R.S. Chap. 17	 $ 730,000
Public Service Retirement Act	 775,000

I wish to bring to the attention of the committee that since a year ago this expenditure has been increased by $355,000. There has been a saving of $55,000 under the other heading, leaving a net increase of $300,000 in one year. Under this, of course, come the retirements from the various departments. Before I deal with that subject, however, let me point to a still more striking fact. In 1921-22 the
Supply-Public Works

figure was $760,000; to-day it is $1,505,000. In other words, in the space of three years the expenditure under superannuation has increased by $745,000. That we may appreciate the significance of this, let me take a couple of departments, the cost of which is very largely in the employment of help-wages. The Customs department, for instance, over the same period, has increased in cost $3,272,000; the Post Office Department, $1,710,000.
Do those figures cover both salary and superannuation?

I am speaking of the cost of running the departments. I have cited these two departments as illustrations anH to emphasize the necessity of the government being brought as early as possible to a realization of where we are drifting with these expenditures. While we are told from time to time that there is a reduction in the estimates- $19,000 in this case-yet we find in the Public Works department there is an increase in superannuation of some $75,000 for last year, showing that as a matter of fact the cost of carrying on the department has really increased by about $55,000 or $60,000. And this in face of the declaration of the government that they are economizing, that the cost of operation is actually being reduced.
Now, take the minister's own department. It is not my desire to offer any very sharp criticism of his staff, hut I do say to him that certainly the Public Works department is not increasing its activities, consequently there is no need for an increase of staff, and I think we could afford-shall I say?-to carry on with a smaller staff. I am not asking the minister to discharge a lot of his employees, but I do suggest that when he retires a man or woman, as the case may be, he should not fill the vacancy until it is absolutely necessary. In other words, he should not pass a civil servant over to the superannuation fund under the Finance department estimates and then immediately appoint another person to the position thus created. It will he noted that the number of employees has been reduced by only four during the past year. This condition permeates the whole service and increases the cost of carrying on the affairs of the country, so that unless we do something in (the nature of definite retrenchment I do not know where we are going to drift. A few days ago the hon. member for 'St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) in the course of a speech divided the national expenditures into what he called controllable and uncontrollable. Here is undoubtedly controllable expenditure. We are not now in the realm of statutory expenditure 
such as the public debt interest, we are in the realm of controllable expenditure, and under that head, notwithstanding that there is a contraction of demand upon the department for service with a diminishing expenditure on public works, the cost of running (the department is kept up to this very high level, with the result that the so-called economy is wiped out two or three times over by simply adding to the superannuation estimates for all of the departments $745,000 during the last two or three years.

Are not the retirements
fixed by statute?

Certainly, the superannuation is paid out under statute. When I speak of controllable expenditure I refer to this vote of $614,000 now under consideration. In order to clear up any misapprehension, I am pointing out that this is the class of expenditure which we must expect to cut down if we are going to effect any economies, and again I say to the minister, I am not arguing for wholesale dismissals, but I do submit that when the minister retires-as he did last year-186 employees, it is not necessary to fill all the vacancies.
How do the vacancies filled compare with the retirements?

The minister could not
give us that information yesterday.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. H. KING (Kootenay, Minister of Public Works):
speechtext: Pardon me, I gave information as to retirements and the positions refilled under Civil Government.

I am not blaming the minister, as he would have found if he had waited a moment. He could not tell us because the 186 include not only those in the inside service in Ottawa but others scattered throughout the country. I was going to add this information. that.

retirements from the inside service.

Supply-Public Works
at Ottawa. There were 174 retirements from the outside service. But let me emphasize this for a moment. In all the departments, from day to day and from week to week there are retirements, and there are those, perhaps, who give up their positions. On the other hand there are demands for additional clerical help. It may be on account of a rush of work in the Interior department; it may be a need for extra help for a week or two in some other department. But, instead of drawing upon some department that has a surplus of idle clerical help, appeal is made to the Civil Service Commission and the necessary extra assistance is obtained by additional appointments.

I quite agree that when extra help is required the departments are too prone to call in new recruits. That was my own experience When I was in the civil service. But as things stand to-day, can ithe minister obtain a transfer of employees from one department to another without proceeding through the Civil Service Commission?

I 6peak subject to correction, but I am sure there is nothing in the Civil Service Act or in any other act to prevent the minister of any department from borrowing clerical help from some other section of the service. Of course I am referring to the inside service, at Ottawa.
an instance in his own department that I happen to know of. I am not going to give the names of individuals; I do not want to bring the name of a civil servant in here with the idea of exposing him to ridicule unless he deserves it in a very striking sense; but there were two gentlemen in his department some years ago, both doing the same work, both having about the same amount of service to render. One of them succeeded in getting four assistants, while the other was carrying on the work by himself, and the man with four assistants was getting $1,500 a year, I think, more than the other. When this discrepancy was called to the attention of the authorities-the civil service adjustment board, I think it was-the reply was: "Oh, this man has four assistants, therefore he is entitled to a higher salary than the other man" - although the other man was doing the work without any assistants. Now, that is what is followed all through the service. I know there are many civil servants who are doing their best for the country, working overtime and never saying a word, economizing and keeping their branches well in hand-men of high efficiency. These are militated against by others who are reckless of public economy and who seek to build their branches up to the highest magnitude possible in order that they may bolster up their own importance and incidentally increase their own salaries That is the crux of the whole business.
How long has that been the rule? I know that right up to 1914 it could not be done; it all had to go through the Civil Service Commission, upon requisition duly made.

I cannot go back before
1914 or thereabouts, but I know it was practised in many instances during the war. But if it is not the case let us make it the case as quickly as possible. I am satisfied that it is the case; that the pathway is open; that all it requires is that the departments exercise their authority. Now, what are the interfering influences that are preventing the government from doing this? There are perhaps two or three. There is the desire to give an opportunity to those on the long waiting list to get into the civil service. But there is an influence much more sinister than that, and it is this: under our present system of handling the civil service, we-and when I say "we" I mean the country by its policy; parliament, if you like, by the act; the government by its administration-encourage the head of a branch, by the very nature of our laws, to build that branch up to as large a personnel as he can. I will give the minister

Was the man with four
assistants literally doing work no more difficult than the man without any?
He did his work infinitely less efficiently.

I mean, was his work of
the same volume?
The volume was the same.
The responsibility, and all that?

Yes. This practice, this
habit-because that is what it is-into which we have allowed certain branches of the civil service to drift has cost this country literally millions of dollars, and we are not getting an equivalent service for the expenditure. Further, and worse still and more unjust, perhaps fifty per cent of the civil servants are faithful, loyal, hardworking and efficient, and they, to use a colloquial expression, "get it in the neck ''-that is not parliamentary, but it really fits the case.

What about the other
fifty per cent?
Supply-Public Works

Well, what about them?
Mr. HAMiMELL: Are they inefficient?

I have been trying to tell my hon. friend, if his mind had been open to penetration, that not only are they inefficient but they are taking unfairly from this country literally millions of dollars, That is what I say. If my hon. friend, who smiles at that statement of mine, can give me any plainer language I will use it.

It is plain enough for
me. I thoroughly agree with my 'hon friend.

I do not know whether
that is a compliment to my reasoning or not. Now I am exceedingly serious about this. I know the difficulty of a member standing in the House and criticizing the civil service, and I do want to make myself clear: I am personally acquainted with many jcivil servants-I could name them by the dozen-than whom there are no better men in Canada. But there are a lot of barnacles hanging on to this government and battening upon the rest of the service, and it is about time we got rid of them.

Was that always the
case?

Certainly, to a large
extent.

I quite agree with my
hon. friend, from my own experience in the service, but the present minister is not to blame. Let us get together and I fancy we can weed opt forty per cent of the civil servants and have a better service.

It is a thing that has
grown and grown. I recall that just after the outbreak of war, in 1915, I made a similar statement, but we were plunged into war and abnormal demands were made upon various branches of the civil service, some of which were worked to the point of distraction. That was an inopportune time to step in and make any such segregation. But a few years ago, I think the first year this government were in office, the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Murphy) told the House about some very striking saving that had been made in his department. I have the figures before me and I am going to quote them merely as an illustration-I do not want to branch off into another department, but it will serve to emphasize this very point. The Postmaster General told us the other day that he was making a direct saving; that on account of the introduction of certain machines, which I understand are very good and which I am 
going to examine more closely when the opportunity offers, he had got rid of a large number of employees. But here are the facts, and this is what we have to take as the test of the case: In 1921-22 the estimate of the Post Office Department was 829,533,671; this year it is 831,254,634. The supplementary estimates are not down, but the increase already shown is 81,710,963. What is the use of telling us about introduction of up-to-date machinery and that someone has been lopped off, when the figures show an increase of a couple of million dollars in that one department in a matter of three years? Then, of course, there is an increase of $745,000 in superannuation over the same period. Here are the figures for the Customs department: 1921-22, $6,782,195; this year, $10,054,504, an increase of $3,272,309. Again you have a startling and damning condemnation of the system that we are following-there is something radically wrong with it.
Now what I am trying to point out to the minister is this: Here is a practical suggestion, here is a wholly feasible suggestion, which I think ought to be taken up at once by the government, and not be put off to be considered this year or next; let us take it up now. When vacancies occur in the civil service, turn to some other branch of the service which is over-staffed and draw men from that branch to fill the vacancies. You are then not turning people out on the street. I have heard it stated here in the House, and it has often been replied to me: Oh, you are going to turn these men and their families out on the street-perhaps in the middle of winter;-it is not fair. I admit that, and I am not asking you to do it. But, I say, stop sending out these appeals for new appointees, stop asking the Civil Service Commission to make new appointments, when the help you require can be obtained from some other department. The minister may say to me: Oh, but I want such and such a clerk for such and such a purpose-and I must say that they have some of the most meaningless names possible for some of these positions; I can pick them out at random in any department. I see here for instance, principal clerks, senior clerks, assistant senior clerks, senior quality surveyors, account clerks, law clerks, audit clerks, clerk-bookkeepers, and so on. Take, for instance, an audit clerk or an account clerk or a senior clerk; any one of these ought to be able to do the work of the other. If an audit clerk cannot do an account clerk's work, he is no good; and if an account clerk cannot do an audit clerk's work, he is not fit for his duties,-and I am talking

Supply-Public Works
on a subject I know a good deal about; I would not give you a fig for a clerk who was carried on my books and could not do an audit clerk's work as well as ordinary accounting work, they are both the same. Why have this multiplicity of distinctions, and then when a vacancy occurs among the account clerks, though there may be a dozen audit clerks idle, a new account clerk is brought into the service? Let us sweep aside these cobwebs of formality and dilatoriness, and attack this problem. It can be done, I venture to say that a reduction in the cost of the civil service, and in the cost of administering the affairs of this country, can be made within a year that will surprise both the government and this parliament, if we seriously attack the problem.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Does my
hon. friend suggest that we are not already making transfers of employees from one department to another. That is being done every day. I am not taking any credit for it, but that is actually being done every day.

Then how in the name of common sense does it happen that we hear daily protestations that an effort is being made at redaction, when we find that in this department, which is the one we are speaking of now, though twelve were retired last year, only four less appear here.
That is the inside service.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am referring to the particular statement my bon. friend made, that no transfers are taking place, but that new individuals are being brought into the service.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We do that

But only in a trivial
nuimiber of cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Civil
Service 'Commission have a list of all these people. For example, we send to the commission the names of individuals who are not required in the hope that they will be put into some other department where there is a vacancy. I do not wish to interrupt my
bon. friend, but I wanted to point out that what he is complaining is not done is actually being practised.

Now the minister says
that these vacancies are filled by transfers.
I find that in the Post Office Department in 1924-25 there were 796 employees, and' this year there are 821. I find that in the Public Works Department there is a decrease of four as compared with last year. Let us turn to some other department. We have a shrinkage of one in the Patent and Copyright office, but in the meantime retirements have occurred: I do not know how many have occurred in Ottawa; I have been trying to get that information all session; I asked the commission for it; I asked the Statistical branch for it, and I also asked one or two of the ministers when their estimates were up, but I have not been able to get the information. All this information should have been laid on the table. I have under my hand the retirements from the Public Works department, outside and inside, showing retirements as follows: in 1921, 57; 1922, 54; 1923, 54; 1924, 186; or a total of 351 retirements in four years from that one department. But now I oome back to the point I made before. Although you have had 351 reitiramlents from this one department alone, and they are costing the country $147,515 a year, the cost of running the department is going up; most certainly it is not shrinking. The minister may not have been in his seat when I said this before and I will repeat it for his benefit. In the Post Office Department there is an increase of $1,700,000, and in Customs an increase of 83,272,000, over the cost of two yeans ago. So where are you going to find the vallue of the retirements and the vacancies?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not finding fault with my hon. friend for his criticism of the increase in the Civil service; that is his privilege. All I want to say to him is that he will find as the years go by and as Canada and the business of Canada grows, there is bound to be an increase. But I want to make it plain that the particular matter of which my hon. friend complains- that there are no transfers being made from one branch to another-is not correct, for that is being practised to-day. True, it has not been practised very long, but it is in practice at the moment in the civil service.

I will reiterate what I have already said, and add to it this: The very mental attitude the minister takes to my suggestion is unfortunate. The minister's
Supply-Public Works

attitude is to justify everything. I tried to point out a moment ago that it was evident there was something wrong in, the situation, and for heaven's sake-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: For heaven's sake do not put me in the position of justifying it. I agree with my hon. friend, that it is a good thing transfers should take place rather than bringing new blood into the service, and that is taking place to-day.

I wish the minister had listened to all I had to say from the start, and then he would have realized my point when he did pick me up. I do not wish him to steer me off the track. I have a practical and wholly non-partisan suggestion, one that I think will be accepted by all parts of the House. I tried to point out that there has been undoubtedly a shrinkage of service in this department. I said further, that I did not ask the minister to discharge employees from his department and throw them on the street without notice; but I do say, what in the name of common sense is the use of superannuating 12 employees on the inside and 170 odd on the outside, and then refilling their positions? That is not the exercise of good economy. Let me go back to figures for the benefit of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart). As a matter of fact, this year the estimates show a shrinkage of $19,000 but there is represented in another account namely, superannuation, some $75,000. So that there is no saving at all. Chap. 17, $730,000" and "Public Service Retirement Act, $775,000." In regard to the Public Service Retirement Act the present government takes no responsibility for the enactment of that measure, although we are responsible for its administration; the act was the creation of my hon. friend's government which brought it into force in 1920. It was stated definitely in the House last night by an hon. gentleman that it had been a very bad act, and that it 'had led to extravagance. I am not so sure about that. There is a large body of competent men in the service to-day who are doing useful work. They were not in a position to take advantage of the Superannuation Act; and when the late government undertook an investigation, one which was very unpopular, it brought about the condition of which my hon. friend complains to-day.
The classifying of the various positions, with the different titles that were given was done during his time when his government was in office. The Calder Act was introduced at that time in order to take care of men who had worked many years in the service and whom it would be necessary to retire in the curtailment that followed. Actions speak

The minister presented to my suggestion an attitude of justifying present conditions.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend is very good at trying to construe what other people are saying. That cannot be read into any of the language I used. I say most emphatically that I am interested in saving money in the service.
Very good. Let us start from that point.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I simply rose to put my hon. friend aright on one statement he made, that there were few or no transfers going on in the service.

I did not say that: I say, when vacancies occur let us fill them from other branches. The minister said that was being done. I will admit that it may be done in odd cases. If the government does not want to take the responsibility of amending the act, let parliament do so and make it obligatory upon the government to adopt such a policy. That is the only point I was trying to make. I pointed out that it was a habit that had grown up in this country. I quite agree with the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell) that for years and years
we had drifted into a bad habit. I do not say this parliament is to blame more than others, but parliament is to blame if it allows it to drift along. Why can we not frankly face the situation and say that we are prepared to call a halt in these matters? Taking the estimates of the Department of Public Works, we provide $614,000 for 316 employees. It is fair to say that some of those may retire and the full amount may not be required. It would be proper under the circumstances to Lower the estimate a little and allow for retirements of that kind. I am not particularly urging the point, but let us give some evidence, some decision and show a fixed determination to follow the course of practical economy which will reveal itself in dollars and cents in the estimates before the House.

The hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) spoke of the positions dropped. There were ten positions dropped. Six of them will be filled, of which two are new positions. They will be filled during the year, in all probability. And one position will be revived. And there were three persons transferred from the Ottawa building staff.
Has the minister any power to dismiss any of his officials or staff?

The minister may dismiss for cause. The staff, is pretty much regulated by the Civil Service Commission. If we find we have an excess staff we recommend retirement, and that is looked after by the Civil Service Commission.
If there is over-manning the minister will be responsible?

Yes. The staff has been graded and the whole service in each department has been gone over by the commission. They set the number of employees, and place them, and say "This is your duty and your position". And that is the way the estimate is made up, each position having its classification. It is true that the government are responsible for the retirements and increases in the service, but it is done through the commission, and the commission have graded the service as it is to-day.

In the case of a person on the staff as a permanent official, the minister cannot dismiss him-at least, if he does dismiss him the Civil Service Commission take the matter up and give the man a position somewhere else. Is that true?

I think the
government have great difficulty in dismissing officials without cause-at least they could not retire an official and fill the position with another employee or another person.

We hear the statement made by a responsible member of this House, who has had considerable experience, that fifty per cent of the civil service is inefficient and that the staff is largely over-manned. There is no doubt that a feeling exists in the country that the civil service costs far too much. The expenditure of the country is to a large extent uncontrollable, and if we are to practise economy it can only be in those items in which the government has control. We hear about economy, economy, all the time, and yet when it comes to the estimates we find we are just in the same place as before. I question very much if we have as large a population in Canada as we had three years ago, and yet we hear continually about the growing services of the country and the demand for more service. If our population is getting smaller and our service is increasing, where are we going? I do not feel like blaming the ministers too much, because it seems to me they are largely the creatures of circumstances. I like the suggestion of the hon. member from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), .that we should get together and find some method of remedying this state of affairs; cease playing politics altogether and try to find a solution for the whole problem. It is an alarming state of affairs, and the country is up in arms about the cost of government. I sincerely hope that we can find some method of improving matters. I like the suggestion of transferring from one department to another when occasion requires, and I think economy might be effected by not appointing new officials in certain cases. I have no doubt that if anyone familiar with the service would inspect the whole system he would find that there were some departments overworked and others which had not enough work to do. We require business methods to be applied to the civil service in order to remedy the existing conditions.

I do not think
it is a fair statement to say that fifty per cent of the civil servants are inefficient and unrequired.
Not unrequired.

I rise to a point of order. Both hon. gentlemen have wholly misstated my observation. What I said was that fifty per cent of the service was of the very highest

type, the best in the country, men who are faithful and loyal and giving valuable services to the country, and in many cases working freely overtime and long hours. I said it was unfair to this fifty per cent, using the word in a general sense, that a large number of others who were wholly inefficient and unworthy of their positions should make it more difficult for these first-mentioned employees.
I wrote down what the hon. gentleman said and I have it exactly.

The
hon. member from Vancouver Centre rose to a point of order. What was the point?
It was just to get an opportunity to explain to the minister.

It has been the
desire and policy of the government to reduce the service, and I cannot give figures offhand, but I have no doubt they will be given later on in the discussion of estimates. Some thousands in the service of the government have been retired in the last few years. It is true there have been some increases. The postal service and the customs service have been increased, and those services will increase because Canada is growing in population today, despite what some people say. We know there is an increase in population. One has only to consider the school attendance in Canada, and there you will have a pretty good index as to the growth of the population. Those services will undoubtedly increase from time to time. We had a very influential delegation before the government a few days ago, and there have been suggestions in this House that the Customs department were not giving the protection they should and were not preventing smuggling. If the minister is going to give the efficient service he would like to give along the boundary, and in the patrolling of the waters of the Pacific and the Atlantic, to prevent the smuggling and the trafficking that is going on, then there will certainly be an increase in the service and an increase in the expenditure to maintain that service.

Mr. Chairman, as I have already suggested, I do not see why one minister should be put under fire as regards this question of increases in the public service. What has been said by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) is true to a considerable extent; there may not be fifty per cent barnacles in the service, but there are many cases where savings can be effected. The minister in charge of this department is

not responsible for the fact that some members of his staff have taken advantage of the Calder Act. If men who had been in the service for twenty-five or thirty years, and who were not under the provisions of the old Superannuation Act which obtained prior to 1896, had not taken advantage of the Calder Act, they would have had to make a return of five per cent of their salaries to come under tlie new Superannuation Act. Their retirement is not the fault of the minister of any department. I know of men in the Engineering Branch of the Department of Public Wofiks having been tmnsferred from London, Ontario, to Nova Scotia to take engineering positions. Several of us did not like that, but it was done. The minister could) not do anything else. But do not blame any minister for the rotten system which has grown up in this country ever since confederation, undter which every membeT wants to place friends in the service. I think the propeT way is to take the different items, whether for public works or anything else, and1 discuss each upon its merits. Let some hon. member put a resolution on the order paper which will go to the root of the whole matter; let us have a field dlay, laying aside all our party prejudices and party affiliations, and see if we cannot arrive at some method whereby we can have an efficient civil service without increasing the cost to the people, and1 wherever possible get clear of those officials who are not necessary. Because a man has been in the civil service ten, fifteen or twenty years, is no reason whatever why he should be superannuated. The country owes him nothing; he took the job of his own volition. Often, as I have already said, he takes his superannuation and then goes out and competes with other men, knowing he has the country behind him for sometimes four, five, six or seven thousand dollars a year. For instance, I db not think a judge, after he gets superannuation should be able to hold any other public office in this country.

What about a deputy
minister?

He is in the same
category. I contend that any man who has taken advantage of superannuation on account of ill-health, age or any other reason should not be permitted to enter public service again. We had/ experience of that in the Minister of Justice of the late administration.

I wish to say to my
hon. friend from Hants (Mr. Martel 1) that members do not get salaries, they get indemnities.

In my own case and
that of my friend (Mr. Carroll) it is only salary for a little lost time, and then it does not half pay us. I contend that the public owe no man a living, and no man has a right to be a sponger upon his fellow citizens. Any man who can do an honest day's work with brain or hand can earn a living in this country. It may not be an excellent living, but it all depends upon the ability andi energy of the individual. But, coming back to the point, why attack one minister because of certain things over which he has absolutely no control? I agree with my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), and I speak from experience. In the civil service there are tots of hard-working, honest, upright men and women who are prepared to work from nine in the morning to twelve at night, if necessary, to carry on their duties; I can point out such people in the Department of Marine and Fisheries. But I have seen officials who simply wrote out checks or put letters in envelopes, for which they drew $2,500 or $3,000 a year, watch the clock and at the proper time take their canes in hand and walk away, andl half the day they were considering how they could agitate for more salary. That is the type of civil servant we have to get after. If no one else will do so, I will place a resolution on the order paper so that we may have a field day and discuss the subject thoroughly. In the meantime do not let us condemn a minister for a system that he did not create.

Has the minister power to
dismiss civil servants, provided he is convinced that his department is over-staffed? If so, is such procedure often followed?

Where retirements have occurred we have tried not to refill the positions. If a deputy minister finds his department over-staffed and recommends to the minister that it be reduced, the minister would send his deputy's recommendation to the commission. The commission, I have no doubt, after investigation, would accept the recommendation.
Mr. Chairman, I do not understand that my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) is making an attack upon the Minister of Public Works,-
I do not think so.

-but he is drawing the attention of the committee to a situation which I think ought to be ventilated. There could not be a more severe indictment of the civil service than we have had from t h'

member for Hants (Mr. Martell), and he speaks as one haying knowledge and experience, he speaks from the inside of the service and tells the House and the country what we all know, and what the country suspects rather than knows, that a considerable proportion of the civil service in this city are simply time-killers, drawing their checks and doing mighty little in return.
One of the things I object to most has been referred to by my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre, and it touches the point raised by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke). He says: Let us get politics out of the civil service. Why, Mr. Chairman, there is more politics in the civil service than there is in the Liberal party, the Farmer's party or the Conservative party. There are men in the civil service who are playing politics all the time. I do not mean party politics.

They are playing their
own politics.

Yes, and they get around them certain groups. One deputy minister says to another, "You help me here and I will help you there." Another says, " I am not getting what I should get; cannot we form some association and boost ourselves?" There is more politics in the service than in this House, in my judgment. I have seen what my hon. friend refers to-a man having charge of a branch will build it up with an unnecessarily large staff in order that he may be able to say to his minister, " Why, I have so much responsibility, I have ten people to look after." But perhaps his whole staff are simply supernumeraries, they should not be there, and if he were an energetic and faithful civil servant they would not be there. Everybody is boosting his salary. I do not think the Minister of Public Works can accomplish a reform here. If reform is to be achieved it must be undertaken by all the ministers of the government working together; the government as a body must decide on clearing out unnecessary officials, and to do this they must go through the service ruthlessly. By that I do not mean that they are to deal unjustly with any civil servant; but they should cease filling vacancies. I suggested in this House four years ago that the government of that day-which is not the government of to-day-should declare a holiday in appointments for three years. I think that could have been done then, and I think it can be done now. Whenever there is a position to be filled, with perhaps some rare exceptions in the case of highly technical help being required, a member of the sendee

can be transferred to it if it is absolutely necessary to fill the vacancy. In the course of a couple of years you would reduce the sendee by about a thousand at least and you would save a large sum of money. I have had a question on the order paper for a month and have not yet been able to get an answer: I want to know how many appointments were made by the Civil Service Commission in 1924. That should not be a difficult question to answer, but it would be very interesting information for the House to have. I do not know when the question is going to be answered-

Does the hon. member mean
new men coming into the service?

Yes. The question I have on the order paper is as follows:
How many appointments were made to the civil service of Canada by the Civil Service Commission during the calendar year 1924?
I propose to get an answer to that question if it can be had. I know that a good many hon. members to my left

not many across the way, I am sure-have a high opinion of the value of the Civil Service Commission. I think it is a waste of money. I said that when I think I was the only member on my side of the House who said so. But everything I predicted about that commission has been fulfilled. They can remain in existence only by making appointments; the more appointments they make, the more work they can show they are doing. Their whole interest, their permanence, really, as part of the civil service of Canada, rests upon the making of new appointments. Why should they not make appointments? Why should they not be one of the influences that are making for filling up instead of cutting down?
When the hon. member speaks of filling up, making appointments, does he mean that the Civil Service Commission have the right to create positions?

No. It comes back to this: here in the service they are playing politics. The Civil Service Commission wants to stay in business. The commission and their staffs have great influence with the deputy ministers, assistant deputy ministers, senior clerks and all the rest. These people owe something to the Civil Service Commission, and the influence that is working is upon every deputy minister and assistant deputy minister to ask that appointments be made here, there and everywhere, which gives a job to the Civil Service Commission and enables it to stay in business. We are spending over $300,000 on that commission.

makes a mistake in offering all these suggestions in public.

Well, it is not the first
time I have made them in public. I do not know just what my hon. friend objects to.
I am stating what I believe to be the facts.
They will follow the suggestions.
Follow what suggestions?
The commission and the different departments are following your suggestions.

If my hon. friend1 knew
the Civil Service Commission he would not be under the impression that they needed any suggestions from toe; they can give me cards and spades and beat me even then. I say it was a mistake to appoint them. As long as you have the commission an existence you are not going to be able to cut out the unnecessary timber in the civil service. What is required in connection with the civil service is pruning. We ought to have a prime minister of the same courage as the president of the United States who says he is going to reduce the cost of government in that country; he is going to start at the beginning and make an impression right from the start. The president is reported to have stated that he is going to cut the cost of the service to a sum that will make the taxation in that country $25 per capita, while in Canada it is $47 per capita. If that does not give the members of the government cause for serious consideration, then I think it ought to. This country cannot pay twice the taxation that is being paid across the border and hope to compete with that country. The thing to do with the civil service is to reduce the expenditure by about $10,000,000. I have not gone into the figures so as to be able to say to what extent it can be reduced, but I am satisfied it can be cut much to the advantage of the country. We had this Civil Service Commission go through the service and classify every job. Well, how did that work out? This way. Here is a man who was classified as junior clerk. He gets everybody he can-his superiors, and those on the commission-to work to have him advanced a stage. He gets up to senior clerk, then he wants to be special clerk or assistant to the assistant-assistant to the deputy's assistant. There is no stopping place for a man of that type in the service, but there is a stopping place for the man who is intent upon his work and is doing it instead of simply trying to boost his own salary and to do as 54
little work as he can. The politician in the civil service is the man who does not work and who is always pulling somebody's leg to get something more for himself. And, of course, every case of that kind is taken up by the commission, it is investigated and reported upon, and that all bulks largely in the work of the commission and adds to its superficial importance. I think a committee of the cabinet, perhaps associated with the deputy ministers, could reduce this service enormously, could get rid of the drones and put it on a better basis. You would get rid of the drones if they were in your business. No other business could be carried on the way the government of Canada is carried on.

Two years ago
there was a meeting of the full cabinet with the deputy ministers and the Civil Service Commission and the suggestions my hon. friend is making were made then to the head of each department. They were impressed with the extreme necessity of reductions wherever possible.

Perhaps the minister will
show us what the result was.

It will be shown. This discussion is foreign to the vote, and the vote under which it would be in order will come up later. However, I have no objection; this will be merely a wanning-up for the main discussion.

good results have followed, according to the estimates which are before us to-day. While it may not be strictly in order, I do agree with the hon. member (Mr. Hocken) that no subject is of more significance to the people of Canada than that of the civil service. Anybody who has the least acquaintance with the facts will readily admit that not only is there considerable overmanning in the public service, but, what is perhaps even more important, there is overlapping as between departments. The system we are following at present is a somewhat complicated one. We have a Civil Service Commission appointed for the purpose of in-

quiring into the abilities of individuals to fill positions, and also charged with the duty of filling those positions. They have the power to determine qualifications, and likewise the power of appointment. They have absolutely nothing to do with the creation of new positions nor with the elimination of existing positions; the duty of creating or eliminating positions in the public service rests entirely with the cabinet council.

Has the commission no
power to advise on that?

They may have power to
advise, but they have no power to act on those questions. It appears that while the commission have the power of appointment, they have not the power to discharge; that power rests entirely with the council. Two years ago we had an opportunity in a committee of considering this very important matter, and I think everyone was impressed with the necessity of doing something, because it was realized that a very substantial amount of money would be saved to the people of Canada if overmanning and overlapping in the service could be prevented. I made one suggestion to the committee and I want to offer it to the House. Sometimes we cannot be a lamp unto ourselves, but there is no reason why we should not borrow a little oil sometimes from neighbouring institutions. There has developed of recent years in the United States a form of government for municipalities known as the business manager system. It has given satisfaction, and it is being rapidly established in some of the largest cities in America. Indeed, some of our own cities in Canada have adopted that plan. Now, is it not possible to make a proper adaptation of that plan to the civil service of Canada? I think it is. If I understand the constitution aright, the general manager of the services of Canada, including the civil service, is the Prime Minister of this country; that is his particular task. But, owing to the fact that he is charged with large problems of state and problems of policy, it is impossible for him to give to the civil service, for example, the detailed consideration that is necessary. Suppose, for example, that he delegated that function to a business manager or general manager who had supervision over the entire civil service, who had complete and final authority not only to eliminate overmanning, but also to prevent overlapping in the departments;-and when I speak of overlapping let me illustrate what I mean. I do not know that this situation now exists; I know it existed two or three years ago. Take the important 
public service of dredging. That was carried on two years ago by three departments of government, the Public Works department, the Marine and Fisheries department, and the Railways and Canals department. Each department has certain jurisdiction, in the St. Lawrence river. The St. Lawrence ship channel, the middle of that river, up and down which ocean ships come and go, is dredged by the Marine and Fisheries department. From the boundaries of the channel to the boundaries of the river on either side the dredging is done by the Public Works department; whereas the harbours are dredged by the Railways and Canals department. Now what business organizations would tolerate a situation of that kind for a single moment?

The Railways
and Canals department would dredge only harbours connected with railway terminals, and so forth.

Quite right. I take it the
harbours connected with the railwiays would be dtedged by the Railways and Canals department.

Only those in
which they have a direct interest.

They would have a direct
interest, for instance, in the harbour of Quebec and in the harbour of Montreal.

They would not
do any dredging there.

Probably not, but I have
given two departments that do dredging in connection with the St. Lawrence river. I have heard that these three departments met at Port Nelson on Hudson bay to do dredging up there. Each found themselves armed with authority from their department, and each department refused to let the other department do the work, and the result was the work was not done that year. I do not know what truth there is in that statement, but in any event the example I have given will illustrate my point. Here are three departments with three sets of officials and three groups of equipment, all for the one purpose of dredging. Why should not one department alone be charged with that service? There would be a great deal saved not only in the way of eliminating overmanning, but also by preventing overlapping were that suggestion adopted. Now my suggestion is this, that we should have a general manager of the service, a man charged with the task of preventing all appointments of additional unnecessary men, a man who has

I want to say now that so far as the theory of the Civil Service Act is concerned, I am in hearty accord. There are two vital principles that we must not forget in the creation of that act; one is the application of the merit principle to positions in the public service; it is essential that political patronage be eliminated. The merit system should apply so that those who are best qualified will get the positions that are vacant.
How would you apply that to minor positions in the country?

I can only tell my hon.
friend that in the United States they have not any difficulty in applying that system even to the lowest-paid service, and apparently they are applying it with satisfaction.
How could that be done?

If you will give me the position you want filled, I will indicate how it is done. I do say that the merit principle is fundamental. The second principle involved in connection with the operation of the Civil Service Act is that an independent body, a non-partisan body, a body freed from political control, should have the carrying into effect of the merit principle. Now, I am frank to admit, that in my humble judgment the civil service commissioners have failed in their duty, and I think they are chargeable before the people of this country for their failure to properly apply these two principles. I do not hesitate to say to hon. members of this House that I had thought that probably the proper thing to do was to present a resolution before the House advocating the discharge of these commissioners. But the failure of these officials to perform their duties is altogether different from saying that the merit system should not apply. I think in the Civil Service Act a mistake was made in appointing three commissioners. I think only one should 54i
have been appointed, and this country should have been searched high and low in order to get an individual to fill that position who would have commanded the confidence and the esteem of this country. I think that in the application of the merit principle to the services of Canada we made a very sad mistake at the outset in restricting ourselves to political considerations in filling these high positions.

How would you apply the merit system to the outside service where a competitive examination is really a matter of form, and where one man is just as well qualified to fill a vacant position as another?

If my hon. friend thinks there should be a separate test applied-for example to an audit clerk who wants a position in Ottawa-I think he is entirely mistaken. If a test is necessary it should be applicable all over the country, and not restricted to applicants for positions in the city of Ottawa alone.

My hon. friend has not grasped my point. I did not refer to such positions as audit clerks, bookkeepers, and the like; I was referring to lighthouse keepers, lock tenders, or occupations of that kind throughout the country, in regard to which my hon. friend must admit the qualifications of one man are just as good as those of another. I do not see that the merit system would be of any benefit in such cases, and to put in force a costly and elaborate system of competitive examinations for the selection of men to fill these positions is entirely unnecessary. I should like my hon friend to give us his opinion on that point.
There must be ten or twelve thousand such positions that are entirely exempted from the provisions of the Civil Service Act.
No, no.
Anything below $200.
Anything below $200 is exempted from the provisions of the act but positions carrying with them a higher wage are subject to the Civil Service Commission.

The hon. member (Mr. Maclean, Prince) gave a concrete example of the class of cases he has in mind. He referred to the position of lock tender, and there are possibly one hundred lock tenders in my county. Would the hon. member kindly state what qualifications the Civil Service Commission have for making these appointments?

If it is merely a labourer's position my suggestion is that the Civil Service Commission adopt the plan which is followed in many states of the American Union: Simply have some qualified official, already in the public service, decide the fitness of a particular individual for any task however minor it may be.

What about hon.

I think hon. members should ask to be excused from all such duties. As I understand a member's duty he is not elected for the purpose of filling minor positions in the public service, nor, for that matter, any position. What I had intended
to say has been well covered already by Other speakers. However, I should like to stress one phase of the question. We have heard a good deal about the necessity for a reduction in the number of public employees. I am absolutely convinced of the necessity for such a reduction. But what are we to do in the face of the situation I am going to describe. Let me give an illustration, it will be very familiar to every hon. member. As I drew my mail from the post office box this morning I pulled out a couple of familiar brown envelopes. I think we receive practically every day a brown envelope sent out by the Civil Service Commission containing a notice asking for applications for men who will take examinations for a certain position. These requests come pretty nearly every day, all the year round; the commission is continually flooding us with these notices. What does it mean? It means that every year, every month, every day the people of this country are being invited to apply for entrance into the civil service. Now, in view of the fact that the ministers are continually making the statement-and in 5 p.m. many instances the statement is correct-that reductions in the service are being carried out, and that there are so many fewer employees in individual departments, I wonder what becomes of the thousands of misguided applicants who seek

admission into the public service? What happens to them after they take their examination? Does it mean that notwithstanding the protests on the part of the members of the government, notwithstanding the express desire of the House itself, notwithstanding the growing intensity of feeling throughout the country for the practice of economy, the civil service is actually increasing and growing all the time? I think a very sound suggestion has been made that for two or three years the issuance of these brown envelopes shall cease, and that if men are required in a particular department the proper officers in that department shall go to another branch of the public service and say "Can you spare us a man, because the law will not permit us to bring another person into the service?" I believe that would be the soundest way to proceed. I realize the difficulty of saying to a man who has been in the service of the country for many years "You are no longer necessary, you must go;" but nevertheless through deaths, sickness and retirements it is possible to reduce the number of appointments, and I would suggest that we should make a hard-and-fast rule for a certain time that these brown envelopes should stay at home, and that no more applications for admission to the service shall be sought for that period and no more admissions permitted. Let us try that system, and also endeavour to fill vacancies necessary to be filled by transfers from other departments.

I have a word to add to
the discussion in the way of a suggestion. The matter is of interest to the country generally, and if you ask citizens at large what they think of the public expenditure along this line they will ask "Why is not something done?" But the system complained of goes on year after year and nothing is done. I am told by a certain person who is an authority on these matters-I do not claim to be an authority myself-that one method that would be helpful in the reduction of expenditures would be along this line-I think perhaps the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) may have referred to it:	When
positions need to be filled supernumeraries should be transferred from departments where the volume of business is less than it formerly was. I am told that the work of some departments was quite extensive years ago necessitating the employment of a certain number of men, but of recent years the business has fallen off and! yet the same sized staff is maintained althrough in certain cases the men are no longer needed. I suggest that those men Who are drawing their salary and

Because the need for economy is urgent and has been urgent for some years. I am not saying that in this case the Minister of Public Works has had sufficient opportunity _ to do that, but in many departments the ministers can take that step. I make these few remarks, because I believe that in doing so I am voicing the thoughts of ninety-five per cent of the citizens of my constituency and, indeed, of my province.
Would the hon. member be in favour of scrapping the whole Civil Service Act and the Civil Service Commission and starting out anew?

No, I would not. I am
not one of those who believe you can create something after a great deal of thought and work, and then, in some fit of mental aberration, wipe it out entirely and create some new structure. That is what they tried to do in Russia and they failed. We have an existing institution which has a great deal of merit. It has made some reforms which have been of advantage to the country. In my judgment, the proper course to take is to correct the deficiencies of this institution as we have it. By experience they can learn where the weak spots are, and by aggressive action on the part of those in control, they can eliminate the weak spots, transform them by strong methods,
and enable the commission to carry on the work. Let us keep the structure that we have, develop it, build it up and make it more efficient, so that it can, perhaps, effect greater economies.

I find myself much in harmony with the hon. member (Mr. Ladner) in regard to the civil service. Our aim and object should be to develop rather than to destroy. The Civil Service Commission was created on account of a desire for it in the country. The change of officials with every election was something that the people of Canada were heartily sick of. There was a point, I believe, that was missed by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) when he spoke of this continual deluge of brown envelopes. Most of those competitive examinations mean simply a readjustment within the service itself, and the elimination of those would be one of the first things to destroy confidence in the whole system. For instance, a man may be working in the Customs department, and a position is opened up in the Department of Finance. Supposing this man who is looking for promotion is entitled to that, it is only through a competitive examination that promotions and readjustments can be effected in the civil service. The question has been asked here this afternoon who should appoint men in the outside civil service, such men as those attending the locks on our canals. I would say that the only official to appoint them would be the man under whom they are working, the man responsible for their actions. Take, for example, the position of postmaster. There is no competitive examination for the position of postmaster. But the matter is left, in almost every case of which I have known, to the post office inspector of the district, the man who should know the necessary qualifications, the man who visits the district. If there are four, five or six applicants, as there are in most cases, he will interview the men, find out something about their educational qualifications, their ordinary business ability, their standing in the community from the point of view of integrity and in other regards, and he will make his recommendation to his department. Those recommendations are forwarded to the Civil Service Commission, and in every case I have had occasion to look into, the recommendation of the post office inspector has been accepted by the commission. That is perfectly right. The Civil Service Commission is subject to a good deal of criticism from the fact that many sections of the country want the old party privileges again,

patronage and nothing else. I would like to see some members come out more frankly and state what is in the back of their minds, because I think that is what it is.

show that, as a result of the Civil Service Commission, better or more efficient men have been appointed to office than was the case when they were recommended by members of parliament, representative of either of the two old parties in this country?

That would be impossible. If I quoted figures, the hon member for Hants would not accept them. Naturally, he would think the man 'whom he was responsible for recommending would be more efficient than the other.
Nobody expects figures.

It is impossible to deal with a technical question like that, but I believe public opinion on the whole throughout the country endorses the principle of the Civil Service Commission. It may be that the commission is not perfect, indeed, we know it is not, and I believe a good deal of politics is played within the Civil Service Commission as the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) has just said. I believe very frequently where they want a certain man in a particular position, he is put in temporarily and is given an opportunity to become acquainted with the duties of that office, and by and by, after six or nine months, when a competitive examination is called, he certainly is in a preferred position. Many faults can be found with the Civil Service Commission in that regard, but I believe public opinion, on the whole, throughout the country, is in favour of the principle of the Civil Service Commission. And my knowledge is not entirely confined to the west; I find the same feeling at Ottawa.
I find it in my home in the Maritime provinces. I have never been in Hants county; the same feeling may not exist there.

I am afraid the hon.

ing for public opinion in this country as I know it, I believe it is behind the principle on which the Civil Service Commission was based. Let us get behind the principle. There are six more to-day than there were in 1911-12, and I venture to say that there were more public works going on in this Dominion at that time than there are to-day.

That is true.
But methods of business are entirely different to-day; more people are employed in office work than ever before, 'and that is true also of the commercial or business world. I think the comparison of the figures to-day with those of 1911-12 is fair and favourable to the department.
I am afraid I will have to question the minister's statement that in all walks of life there are more men doing the same work to-day than there were in 1911.
In the commercial world, I mean.
I dlo not imagine that in the Canadian Pacific Railway Company's operations, for instance, more men are doing the same work to-day than were employed in 1911.

In their offices,
yes.

Well, this is not only
offices.
Yes, it is the inside service.

At any rate, I would point out that there is throughout the whole of this country a demand, and I think a just one, that we should cut down not only the expense of government but the national expenses generally, Dominion, provincial and municipal. There is a way of cutting down our civil service expenditure; perhaps it was suggested when I was out of the room. I do not believe we should go out into the different departments, and slash here, there and everywhere, put men out of work and increase the unemployment which unfortunately is worse at this time, to my mind, than it ever was in the country before. I am not blaming on the present government, the overloading of the civil service as it prevails in very many of the departments; all past governments permitted the civil service to be built up to a greater extent than it should have been. We cut down the number of employees in the Printing Bureau with good effect and there is no doubt that all the departments, or most of them, could be cut down with resulting improvement to the service and saving to the country.
How did the government cut down in 1911 when 11,060 Liberals who were dismissed were replaced by 33,000 Conservatives?
I do not know that that is the fact, and I shall not be able to discuss it, for that reason. I am not admitting that we did any such thing.
My hon. friend was a Liberal in those days.

Probably I would have agreed with my hon. friend in 1910-11 about that, if it occurred. I do not like to keep repeating to my hon. friend that I am getting wiser as I get older. My suggestion is that when a man retires, dies or otherwise leaves the sendee, let the positions remain as they are or fill them by transfer from some other department.

Supply-Public Works
I think that is being done.

Well, I do not. I hope it is, but I cannot see it in any of the figures. The Postmaster General announced the other day that he had put in a lot of machines to cut down labour, but the fact is that the number of employees in his department has been increased. Certainly ,1 should think there were more than four superannuations or deaths in the Department of Public Works last year. The hon. member (Mr. Stevens) tells .me there were 12, so that the plan I suggest has not been carried out. We certainly could cut down the civil service gradually and work hardship to no one if we adopted this plan of filling vacancies by transfer from the same department or from other departments, and it might then be possible to establish the civil service upon something reasonably like the basis of strength of a private corporation. The minister says that is being done. Well, I hope a real attempt is being made to do it; at any rate, I think there should be a greater attempt than is shown in most of the departments. I admit that the minister's department shows a decrease, but in most of the other departments there appears to be an increase.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Not in mine.
