speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: I hope the hon. member will commend me for reducing my staff.

I hope there will be something upon which we can commend my hon. friend. I repeat that we should make a greater effort than is being made at the present time-and I say it in all sincerity- to cut down the expenses of government and in that way to reduce the very high taxation we have in this country.

That the Civil Service Commission has failed to gain the confidence of the people of the country has been due, I think, to other reasons than their inefficiency. It was noticeable at the first session of this parliament I attended that the Civil Service Commission were getting no sympathy or co-operation from the heads of government, not even from the deputy ministers. Indeed, I have known that from divisional heads the Civil Service Commission has met with opposition in carrying out its wishes. Now this is not as it should be. The hon. member for West Toronto has said that the
Civil Service Commission has no way of finding out an applicant's integrity or his standing in his own community. I can very well remember conditions as they were when the old patronage system was in full swing, and I can assure the hon. member that at that time men were placed in most responsible offices whose integrity to say the least was very questionable.

Those are the men we
are superannuating now.

What happened to the
member appointing them?

Often it is not the member
of parliament that makes the appointment. Can anyone say that I have the patronage in my constituency?
Did the member of parliament who appointed them win his election?

If the member happened to be on the 'opposition side, he had no say in the patronage at all; it was not given to him. In fact, the Minister of Agriculture is the ruler of Saskatchewan to-day. But this is what I want- to tell the House:	I believe
that if the Civil Service Commission to-day had the sympathy of the heads of the government and of the divisional superintendents, and so on, we could make the commission the best system for appointments to the civil service that this country has ever seen. I want also to say ithat the people back in the country will not stand for the abolition of the Civil Service Commission just now.
Don't delude yourself.

I want to make a few remarks regarding the Civil Service Commission. I have been a great deal interested in the remarks that have already been made, and I agree with a large part of what has been said, though I am not in favour with the total abolition of the Civil Service Commission. That commission was appointed some years ago, and it has given' good service to the country, but I think its powers and privileges are altogether too wide, and that the outside service should never have been brought under it. In appointing officials to the outside service, the Civil Service Commission is utterly unable by a technical examination to find out who is the best qualified man for the position. They may be able to ascertain his educational qualifications, but they cannot possibly tell whether he has any ability in meeting the public, or whether he has any knowledge of the details of the department in which the vacancy occurs; nor can they tell anything

Supply-Public Works

about his integrity. They can only ascertain these things by applying to some person in the constituency where the appointment is to be made. Now under the terms of the Civil Service Act a member of parliament is forbidden to make any representations to the Civil Service Commission; I believe a member of parliament is prohibited under a penalty from making any representations to the icom-mittee with regard to any appointment. I believe that if he did make such representations, it would foe against the best interests of the applicant.

Do I understand the
hon. gentleman to say that a member of parliament is prevented from making any representations in regard to appointments to the Civil Service Commission, and that there is a penalty under the act for so doing?

There may not be a
penalty attached, but he is certainly prohibited from making any representations to the commission.
Prohibited by statute or precedent?

There always was a provision in the act that no official of any department could in any way approach a member of parliament and ask his influence to be used in his promotion or anything else. That was in the old act.
A member of parliament is also prohibited from making any representations to the commission regarding the appointment of any person.

Is it not a fact that it was
understood at the outset after the 1918 act was passed that if a member of parliament did approach the civil service commissioners on behalf of any particular person, that person was not to be appointed at all? He was immediately ruled out of consideration. I think that was the intention, but I think it is not observed.

I did not understand
that that was the intention, but I 'have not any doubt that that is one of the results of a member of parliament making representations to the commission. The commission is therefore compelled to apply to some person in the constituency where the appointment is to be made as to the character of the applicant. They must depend upon some person in the constituency who knows the applicant and can say whether or not he is a proper person to be appointed. The Civil Service Commission depend entirely on that, and sometimes they

apply to persons who are friends of the applicant, and who are desirous of seeing him appointed. The consequence is that the commission is very often misled, and the member for the constituency has very frequently to accept the responsibility for the appointment whether he recommended it or not. The public at large seem to think that he has some influence, and that it was through his influence the person got the appointment, and consequently they visit upon him the blame for a bad appointment. Now it is impossible for the commission to know whether a person is capable of meeting the public, whether he is courteous and efficient, or whether he is of good character, and the consequence is that many people are appointed who never should have been.
So far as the inside service is concerned, if you want a reorganization or readjustment made in the departments the one person who knows most about his department is the minister himself. He is the person who should be able to say whether the number of employees in his department can be cut down. He should be responsible for making such recommendations to the Civil Service Commission. He should do that, but under the act I believe he cannot.

Has the minister not
that power? Also what would happen if the minister reduced his estimates after they were brought down to the House?

He cannot reduce his
estimates until he has reduced the number of employees.

If he provided in his
estimates for only a certain number of employees, would not the others automatically vanish?
Not necessarily. They must receive their discharge first. If they are not eliminated from the department and the salaries are not paid where is the minister going to be?
The minister is responsible for his estimates, and not the commission.
The minister can discharge an employee but he cannot appoint one.
He can fire but not hire.

I think the ministers
themselves should take in hand the matter of reducing the number of employees. If you want the civil service cut down, I think you must depend on the ministers at the

p
Supply-Public Works
head of the various departments to do it. One of the criticisms I have to make at the present time in regard to the public service is that while the number of employees in the various departments appears to be increasing the work itself is really decreasing. There is certainly a lack of efficiency somewhere. I think a large number of the civil servants in Ottawa are not fully employed during their working hours; they have a lot of time on their hands and can go out around the city when they should be at work. There should be more work provided for the employees in the public service, and greater efficiency should be required. It is up to the ministers at the head of the various departments to see that these requirements are fully met.

Does my hon. friend
know of one person in civil life who is not employing more men to do the same work than was the case ten years ago?

That may be true.
We have very many more employees in Ottawa than we had previous to the war. The war rendered a lot of additional appointments necessary, and since the close of the war it has been very difficult to get rid of these extra employees. I understand perfectly the difficulty of the government in cutting down the number of additional employees which the war rendered necessary. Although the necessary work in the departments has diminished, it is really difficult to get rid of the extra employees.

My hon. friend has not
answered my question, which referred to persons employed in private life. I know that in Vancouver previous to 1910 I had two persons in the office; now I have six.

I answered my hon.
friend's question. I believe that is true in private life as well as in the government service.

My hon. friend places
the entire responsibility for reducing the staff upon the members of the government. Does he not consider that some responsibility should rest upon the deputy ministers?

The deputy minister,
of course, takes his orders from the minister.

I should like to be set right
in this matter. Assertions have been made indicating that it is not in order for a member of parliament as an individual to make a recommendation on behalf of his fellow citizen who is seeking a position in the public service. I should like to find out from the
minister if that is correct. I do not believe " it is correct. I have always understood that the member's right to make recommendations, as he used to make them, has been taken away; in other words, patronage has been abolished'. But it is absolutely news to me to hear that if a fellow citizen who is seeking a position goes to a member of parliament and asks him to certify to his ability, his integrity and so forth, the latter has no right to do so. I confess I have not done it many times but I have on a few occasions, I think probably six or seven in the last two or three years, written letters of this kind. I am not aware that I did anything wrong in so doing. If so, I should very much like to be put right; I should not like to do anything which was not right in this connection. Generally, as a member of parliament,
I do not do it; I know how useless it would be to entertain any hope of appointing a Tory in my riding; but I have thought that even with a government opposed .to me in politics in office that I could, perhaps, as a citizen, say a word occasionally on behalf of a fellow citizen as to his standing in the community and that it might have some little eff^t. In that capacity I have written a few times.
To whom were the letters addressed?

The letters were addressed
to the Civil Service Commission.
And had they any effect?

Well, now, my hon. friend
is getting a little personal. However, I venture to say my letters have not had as much effect as some he has written.
Mine had no effect at all in favour of the applicant.

Then I venture to say that
my hon. friend has not been as insistent as some of those hon. members who sit beside him, and if he will just exercise a little more energy it will assist him to obtain better results.
May I ask the hon. member a question?

I do not wish to be diverted from my suggestion, but if my hon. friend will possess his soul in patience for a moment he will have an opportunity of putting his question and I will endeavour to answer it. I am really quite serious in wishing to find out from the minister, or from anybody in authority, if I am wrong in the action I took in this matter.
Supply-Public Works

My hon. friend
is quite right. I understand that the act as originally drawn and introduced into the House did prohibit a member from taking such action, but it was amended and to-day it is the privilege of a member, if he so desires, to communicate with or see the commissioners and make such a recommendation. From what we have heard from hon. gentlemen to-day apparently they have not succeeded very well.

Will the minister promise
in the future to intercede on behalf of some of these letters we write?

As a matter of fact, when
an appointment is vacant the member for the constituency receives a special notice from the commission calling attention to the fact that the appointment is in his constituency.

When does the Calder
Act terminate, or has it terminated?

It terminated in
October last. There are no more retirements under that act. Those who retired will continue, of course-
Yes, I understand. The retirements now are under the Superannuation Act, and it looks as though the flock of retirements was multiplied under that act as compared with the Calder Act. Is that a fact?
There have been none in the Department of Public Works this year. I could not say as to the other departments, but I think not-no, none in any of them, I am informed.

There seems to have
been a great exodus in the last few months under the Calder Act. I see men walking around the streets of Ottawa here in the prime of life who have in the last few months taken advantage of the retirement provision. I cannot understand why the government allows those drawing salaries from the administration to multiply. Some of them I knew in the service, and I have in mind some who

Supply-Public Works
were certainly efficient a very short time ago, but they have been allowed to retire, and I presume are hoping, under a change of policy, to get a job in some other line of industry and draw the allowance as well. Of course at the present time there is no chance of that. Is the government considering economy now in any sphere except the relief of the unemployed and hungry?

My hon. friend
could not have enjoyed his dinner. As far as my department is concerned there are no retirements this year. There were fifty-seven retirements in the years 1920 and 1921. It is true that as the act expired many men, especially aged men who would probably be well out of the department as far as their efficiency is concerned, did take advantage of retirements under that act, and, on account of their age and sickness, they were entitled to it. I know that was the strict application we made of the Calder Act.

What about Mr. Drake,
of the Interior department? I know that is not in your department. If he has been ill, I have not heard of it, and I certainly would be surprised to learn that he was entitled to retire of his own free will, on account of age, because he is no older than I am. That is only one case that comes to my mind at the moment. What principle does the minister follow?

My hon. friend will recall that there was a considerable number of employees in the service who, undpr the Calder Act, could retire and secure benefits on retiring under proper conditions, whereas under the Superannuation Act those same men would not be able to retire at all and could not come under that act. Therefore, about the latter part of October last there was a considerable number of those who were old or ill, who did accept what appeared to be their privilege at that time, and chose to retire before October 31. If they had remained1 in the service they would have nothing in sight for themselves at the present time.

It is not they I am thinking of so much as the treasury. I do not think I recollect the Calder Act wrongly, but if I recollect it rightly, no man had an absolute right to retire under it. The government was empowered under certain conditions to accept applications for retirement under that act, and I think rather that the government was empowered to retire arbitrarily of its own will under the act, but I do not think any man had a right to say: "Here, I am going to quit work and draw my allowance under the
act, no matter what the government thinks." Consequently the responsibility for the correctness of the age and other details of these retirements is on the government.

If they made an application for retirement, that went to the Civil Service Commission for consideration and approval, and then came to the minister of the department for approval, the minister to sign the form that was sent to him, already signed by the Civil Service Commission; but I have understood that the onus was largely upon the Civil Service Commission to determine if the claim made for retirement by individual employees was sufficient to justify them in agreeing to the retirement of the employee, and if they so decided the minister seemed to have nothing else to do but to O.K. that proposal of the Civil Service Commission and permit the retirement.
I think the hon. minister is wrong to this extent: he intimates that all the minister had to do, once the Civil Service Commission certified as to the man's position, was to sign on the dotted line.
No; after the Civil Service Commission had determined as to his age or his physical condition as entitling him to retirement,-

No, not entitling him at all. No man is entitled under the Calder Act to retire. I speak with some reserve, but very little. The Civil Service Commission would investigate his representations, and if they found them all right they would say so, and then it was for the minister to say, and I think subject to the approval of council, whether the retirement was actually allowed or not.
Yes.

No doubt the responsibility was on the minister. The minister could plead and! produce any evidence to justify his jurisdiction, whatever was presented by the Civil Service Commission, of course. I cannot understand in the case I have mentioned how the minister could have justified the retirement of the man whose name I have given. I refer to Mr. Drake, a man anywhere between forty-five and fifty-five, an admirable official, appointed by the government previous to the last government; but now, unless he has got a position-and he would be very lucky if he got one just now- he is walking the streets under the Calder Act, and someone else is doing his work and getting the salary. That cannot be attributable to the Civil Service Commission but to this government.
Supply-Public Works

I am not informed of that case. My hon. friend has special knowledge of it. But generally speaking the minister had, of course, discretion, but it went through a form, the application being made was referred to the Civil Service Commission who checked up the years of service and the age of the individual, the health condition, and that was all dealt with under their management, and then the matter came back to the ^minister and each case was considered.
On its merits?

On its merits. I
think that is the course we have been following.

The minister was asked
last night to supply a list of the 186 retirements in his department last year together with the age, so that we might get an idea of the prevailing age at which these civil servants have retired.

I have the list
here. It is very lengthy and could be tabled for the use of members if desired. It shows the name, position, place, reason for retirement, date of retirement, age of retirement, number of years' service, salary at the time of retirement, average salary last three years, gratuity, retirement and annuity, retiring gratuity. That could be placed on the table.

Mr. Chairman, I realize it is a little unfair to ask the minister to give us all those details, but I should like him to take advantage of the liberty usually accorded to a minister and place the information on Hansard.
I can do that if it is the wish of the committee.

Yes. I did not want to embarrass the minister at all.
(For statement see p. 887).

I have the Calder Act before me and I find the Civil Service Commission merely reports on fhe correctness of the facts represented by the applicant. The act says that " the Governor in Council may order that such officer shall be retired," and that " the decision of the Governor in Council thereon shall be final." The responsibility is single, it is not on the commission at all.
The commission prepare the data, make the investigation, which is referred to the minister, and the minister places it before the Governor in Council.

Can the minister tell us what kind of health the animals have now?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this vote is reduced by $95,000. Naturally the query is, do we intend to reduce our activities to that extent. Quite recently we worked out a slightly different system of appraisement of compensation for animals slaughtered for T.B. In addition to that we have ceased to give compensation for certain animals. We are not giving compensation for steers, for the simple reason that 'these animals can be fed and sold at ordinary beef prices. The same applies to animals affected with lump jaw, and to grade bulls.
How is it all right to fatten a tubercular steer and sell it for beef and not fatten and sell a tubercular heifer for beef?
The steer's ultimate destiny is the block, while the female can go on reproducing her species for a long time to come before she goes to the block.

The minister has missed my point altogether, but he has not lost his wit. I have no doubt he can answer this question if he understands it. Suppose a heifer and a steer are both affected with tuberculosis. The minister says, in the case of the female animal the department makes an allowance for its destruction; but in the case of the male animal it is allowed to be fattened and sold as beef. Why not fatten the female and sell it as beef too?

The female is a very much more valuable animal to a man building up a herd. You would be a long time building up a herd on a steer. I think we are perfectly justified. The steer can be sent to the stable for fattening and when it is sold its owner gets full value for the animal. I do not think my right hon. friend wants me to go into more minute details. If he does not know the difference between the two, I am afraid I cannot explain it further on this occasion.

Supply-A gricul ture

Is the beef of these
two animals fit for food?

I think Swift's and Burns's abattoirs are inspected, but small dealers who slaughter their own animals are not controlled at all, their slaughter houses are never inspected. Should not some effort be made, under the heading of the health of animals, if you like, to prevent these dealers from selling the meat of tubercular cattle?

Mr. Chairman, I am
still wanting to know why there is an allowance made for the female animal destined for the slaughter house if it is found to be tubercular, but no allowance is made for a male animal destined for the same place. What is the minister going
to do with regard to the request made to him last August in the town of Carman, Manitoba, by the reeves of three municipalities in the restricted area, Thompson, Dufferin, and Roland-along with them was the Deputy Minister of Agriculture for Manitoba-that the Dominion government assist in meeting the cost of advertising the products from that area? I remember the
occasion, but I think we have gone -pretty far in starting a free area there, the first in the British Empire, I understand. We feel that work of this nature should be worth a good deal to the locality in which it is carried out, and that they should do something to develop their live stock industry along the dine of community breeding or something of that nature. The suggestion was that the municipalities would stand a certain part of the cost of advertising, and the provincial government, through their Deputy Minister of Agriculture, promised to co-operate also if the federal Minister of Agriculture could see his way to assist. My hon. friend did not make any promise, but I am just reminding him of the suggestion that was made to him at that time to see if he feels like doing anything about it. Possibly these gentlemen would only want the services of one man and

Supply-Agriculture

I do not know that that would be very expensive. There is no doubt that they will be anxious to know at this time, when the estimates are going through, if they are to get any assistance along that line. It is a very live question with them

We are working
largely through the Deputy Minister of Agriculture there, Mr. Evans. I have had two or three letters from him. Anything we have had in mind is along the line of the extension of the area to the north; we have not discussed the advertising feature of it. We really could not see our way clear to go that far. I think the local authorities should look after that.

Does the minister promise
that the municipality of Grey to the north is going to be taken into this restricted area?
Not an unconditional promise-if they will do something in the way of community breeding. We lay down that condition. We want to avoid doing too much without their doing something in return.

Yes, if they comply with the conditions laid down.

I believe the impression has gone out that the total vote for health of animals, something like $2,000,000, goes to the reimbursement of owners of animals that have been destroyed on account of disease. How much of this vote actually goes to reimburse owners for the loss of animals and how much to the maintenance of public health, that is, meat and canned foods and the amount expended under municipal orders?

Roughly, the
amounts are divided in this way: Contagious diseases, $1,330,000; meat and canned foods, $520,000; pathological division, $55,000; these divisions subdivided as follows: salaries, $410,000; travelling expenses, $252,000; supplies, $25,000; tuberculosis compensation, $591,000; hog cholera compensation, $4,000; glanders compensation, $7,000; mange eradication, $20,000; rentals, $7,000. The amount expended under municipal orders was $126,000. So that the amount spent for the public health rather than the health of animals would be $520,000 -meat and canned foods-plus the $126,000. Of course, this is all for the health of the human race as well as for the animal kingdom. The compensation is really helpful to man.

I am glad to have this
distinction, because I have heard this vote for $2,000,000 referred to in its entirety as being a vote bo agriculture, whereas this $646,000, as I understand it, is directly for the general human welfare, the balance going to the reimbursement of owners for the loss of animals and the expenses connected therewith. I am heartily in sympathy with this vote, and my only regret is that the government have seen fit to reduce it. I believe that the money that has been expended on the accredited herd system has been probably better spent than any other expenditure the government has made. In the last five years the results from this system and the diffusion of knowledge among the breeders of pure bred cattle concerning tuberculosis have been simply wonderful, and it has been proved beyond a doubt that if the money is expended tills disease can be eradicated. There is not only a great loss in live stock through the carcasses that are condemned, but also a very grave menace to human beings. I believe that in the neighbourhood of Saskatoon something over 10,000 reactors were removed under a municipal order, and every one of these animals was a potential source of disease to the human race.
This money that is expended on the inspection of meat for the protection of the public is also well spent, but I do not think it is anything like so important as the protection of the health of the people from our raw milk supply, because practically all meat is cooked before it is eaten, and the cooking destroys the danger of infection; but raw milk constitutes a very great menace to the health of the public. There is no longer any question that a very large percentage of tuberculosis cases among human beings are of bovine origin, and I only wish there was some method whereby the knowledge that has been diffused among the breeders of pure bred cattle concerning the dangers of this disease could be brought home to the people generally, so that there might come a demand for the expenditure of large sums of public money to protect the health of the people. This may seem to be getting away from the health of animals, but there is such a close connection between the two, and you will notice that the vote takes care of both, that I think I am in order in speaking of the health of human beings on this vote. In certain sections, restricted areas are being cleaned up, but it does seem to me that the best results would be obtained' if we had key herds from coast to coast in much the same way as the accredited pure bred herd system is carried on. I think

in that way good results could be attained in a very few years. It is more important to have this work done in the smaller centres, because in the larger cities there is usually a pasteurizing plant which destroys any danger of infection from the milk; but in the smaller municipalities milk is generally provided in its raw state, and if these small centres were placed on much the same basis as the pure bred herds, the public in the surrounding locality would become aroused to the danger of infection from milk. I suggested 'something like this about a year ago, but it was about twelve o'clock at night when the vote came on, following a long discussion on another phase of this subject. I notice that within the last few days a small municipality that wrote me last year about the subject showing an interest in the vote, has taken steps through its municipal council to provide its citizens with clean milk aside altogether from any assistance from the government. While I agree that great good can be accomplished by having these restricted areas and by municipal order taking in large numbers of cattle surrounding a city I believe that if an expenditure were made from coast to coast by this government, and certain herds that are supplying raw milk and that are a direct menace to public health were taken into an accredited herd system, very good results could be attained in a short time.

Of course, we are
limited in this work by the amount of money available. I might draw the hon. member's attention to the fact that we have over one hundred of what we call supervised herds, which include the grade herds of which my hon. friend has spoken, where a farmer will make application to the Health of Animals branch to have his herd tested by one of our officers. He does not get any compensation, but the test will show him where he stands. The inspector puts a T in the ear of any animal that reacts, and the man then knows exactly what he has got. That costs the farmer practically nothing but he does not get any compensation. There are, however, a considerable number of grade animals for which there is compensation and that is those that are associated with a small herd of pure foreds. For instance, a man may apply to have a small herd of five pure bred cattle come under the accredited herd system, five being the minimum; and he may have 85 per cent of grades in that herd. We will test them in order to protect the pure breds, and allow compensation. So in all these different ways we are covering quite a bit of ground. Before we take any forward step in the direction of cover-55i
ing large areas or an entire province, except perhaps Prince Edward Island, we shall have to secure the co-operation of provincial and possibly municipal governments. There is no reason why the federal government should indefinitely test all these herds free for any city and the city not put up anything towards supplying its citizens with good milk; so we hope to have the sympathies of the provincial and municipal governments enlisted in a practical way, and a system of co-operation adopted that will enable us to go forward. At the moment, times are too hard for most provincial and municipal governments to dip into their treasury for even so worthy a purpose as this. In the meantime we are doing the best we can, but I look forward to having some co-operation with the provincial and municipal governments in the future.

Like the hon. member
for East Peterborough I think this is one of the most important subjects we can discuss in the Parliament of Canada, for it deals not only with the health of animals but with the health of the Canadian people. The minister has stated that we cannot enlarge on this work owing to the fact, that we are a little low in funds. I think it is to the shame of the Canadian people that we cannot find funds enough to take care of the eradication of tuberculosis not only from our animals but from our children also. I am sorry the minister saw fit to increase the grant for experimental farms by $40,000, and at the same time decrease the grant for this work by-SOS,000; so I do niort think all the blame can be attached to the Canadian people. I think the minister should have had courage enough to have given us a grant of perhaps $500,000 more, if necessary, to take care of this work, because after all, w-hile it is a splendid thing to have ornamental hedges, flowering bulbs and forage plants propagated, it is far more vital that we conserve the health of our children. There is no doubt in the world that this disease does menace the health of our people. I have here a poster printed by the Department of Agriculture of the United States-the minister has probably got some of these in his office-depicting a little duld who has been sick by drinking milk from tuberculous cows, alongside a healthy child, a child rendered healthy by drinking milk from healthy cattle. So I say not only does great economic loss result from this disease but it is a menace to public health. I have also figures in regard to the toll this disease takes and the great economic loss which it occasions in the country to the south. In the year 1923, 49,839 head of cattle were slaught-

ered and condemned on account of tuberculosis-they were condemned and thrown into the scrap heap. In the same year 88,688 carcasses of hogs were condemned also on account of tuberculosis. Now the information that we get from this report, bulletin No. 1,069, says that this is probably only about one-half of the total loss in the United States; that only about 35 per cent of the animals killed there are killed in abattoirs besides which many die from the disease. So that the loss given in this bulletin only represents about one-half of the total. I will quote a few extracts from another bulletin on this subject:
What hog tuberculosis is costing farmers
Hog tuberculosis last year sent over 25,000,000 pounds of hog meat into the condemned tanks of only the federally inspected slaughterhouses. This meat, worth, except for tuberculosis, over $2,000,000, was fit only for soap grease or fertilizer.
Hog tuberculosis in one year sent 66,000 hog carcasses into the fertilizer tank.
Hog tuberculosis causes one-fourth to one-third of the hogs shipped from certain inspected farms to be rejected for meat and to be sold at tankage prices.
Hog tuberculosis causes many slaughterhouses in badly infected districts to protect themselves against such losses by offering lower prices for all hogs.
Hog tuberculosis causes other packers to refuse to accept hog shipments from certain dairy districts except as "subject" shipments; that is, "subject" to examination for tuberculosis after slaughter.
Hog tuberculosis, therefore, is causing thousands of farmers to turn their good corn, alfalfa, concentrates, and skim milk into low-priced soap grease instead of high-priced pork.
The bulletin goes on to say that hogs contract tuberculosis chiefly through dairy cows which are also very subject to tuberculosis. The disease in the cow infects her milk, system, her lungs, and her throat with tubercle bacilli.
I have looked over the report of our inspector general and I have compiled some figures which I wish to give, but in doing so I will be as brief as possible. In 1924 we had 11,470 beef carcasses condemned. Over 50 per cent of these carcasses were condemned on account of tuberculosis. At the same time 5,450 carcasses of swine were condemned, and 75 per cent of these carcasses were condemned on account of tuberculosis. I have figured these 5,735 carcasses of beef at a value at $50 a carcass, so we have there a loss of $286,750. I have figured the hog carcasses as worth $18 a Carcass, and the total value would be $73,566.	So there we have a total loss of
$360,316. If we apply the same principle to these figures that is applied in the United States they only represent albtout one-half of the total loss. If you consider that we paid out only a little over $500,000 on account of the accredited herd plan you can

readily see that the economic loss was greater than the amount represented by the monetary paj'iments. And yet some people have the temerity to get up and assert that we are paying out millions of dollars to eradicate this disease. As a matter of fact we are not paying out millions of dollars, we :are only paying out a few hundred thousand a year. Moreover we are accomplishing something through these payments, a fact which the critics referred to ignore.
Now, can we eradicate bovine tuberculosis? I have figures here which will prove beyond a doubt that we can eradicate tuberculosis if we take hold of it man-fashion. Under the municipal testing order in 1923 we tested 54,301 head of cattle, of which 7,976 reacted. The percentage of reactors was 14.7. In 1924 we tested 60,967 head of cattle, there were 3,214 reactors, and the percentage of reactors was 5.3, less than one-half of the number of reactors in 1923 although 6,666 more cattle were tested.
Then under the accredited herd plan which is now in operation, in 1923 we tested 52,548 head of cattle. Of this number 5,484 reacted, and the percentage of reactors was 10.44. In 1924 there were 86,174 head of cattle tested. The number which reacted was 7,343, and the percentage of reactors was only 8.5 although there was an increase of 33,626 in the number of cattle tested, and the cost was less by $2,390 than that of the previous year. This is accounted for, to some extent, by the reduced compensation paid, but mainly by the decrease in the number of cattle which reacted. These facts go to prove that we can eradicate bovine tuberculosis when we tackle the problem in an aggressive way.
We have another ' method in operation in this country-the restricted area system. We have, so far, not branched out very far in that direction but I have some illuminating figures here. In Manitoba the number of cattle tested was 16,550. The number which reacted was 992, and the percentage of reactors 5.8. I have not the figures of all the other tests, I believe there were two others. The first test cost $3.50 per head. The cost of the last test was reduced to 50 cents per head. I think the percentage of reactors was less than one per cent at the time the last test was made. Therefore I make the claim that we can eradicate bovine tuberculosis if we go at it in an aggressive way, and we can save money too if we take hold of the matter in an effective way in time.
The United States have undertaken this work to a greater extent than we have in

Therefore I must express my regret that our government are not keeping step with the United States in this great work. We should be acting on some international plan, we should not only be working in co-operation with the United States but trying to keep up with their efforts. When the United States are taking definite steps to eradicate this disease, we should endeavour to keep pace with them. We find that the Canadian government has accepted that plan and has put it into the regulations^	The	United States	have	another plan. In that country, owners of grade herds can come under the accredited herd plan and take advantage of it in the same way as owners of pure bred herds. I have always wondered why there was this gross discrimination in not accepting grade herds as well as pure bred herds in this country. This seems a	little	like one law for the	richand another	law	for the poor.	Again Iam making	my	plea to-night	that	the
government accept applications from owners of grade herds as well as from owners of pure bred herds. I like to have this
testimony from the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader), because we all recognize that he is a practical live stock man and knows what he is talking about. With regard to the accredited herd plan not being pushed, I do not suppose we are out advertising it, but the complaint comes from Alberta that we are pushing it too rapidly. My hon. friend understands the circumstances. They complain that our inspectors go around canvassing for these herds.
I see no evidence of that.

I am glad my hon. friend says that he sees no evidence of it. We have enough to do without advertising for new herds. When the committee learns that we have 180 herds waiting to be tested, it can readily understand that there is no need of unduly advertising for new herds in Alberta or anywhere else. These applications are coming in at the rate of about forty a week, so that we are behind the applications only about four and one-half weeks. We are therefore reasonably well up to the work. As regards the other places, we try to take them along parallel lines. There is only one area in Quebec, but it takes in a little more than two counties. We have completed the first go-over, and we shall soon have more men liberated so that we shall be able to catch up with these 180 applications. I do not think we can hold out any hope of grade herds being taken on just now, except those that I referred to a few moments ago that were in the same class as the small herds of pure breds. Where a man has, say five pure breds, 85 per cent of grades will be taken on in order to clean up the bunch. I have sometimes wondered whether we are justified in going that far. There is, however, no use in testing such a man's pure breds unless you test his grades and get them cleaned up too. But it is going quite a distance to help the man with a small bunch, and he should proceed along the line of increasing his pure breds rather than of making them an excuse for having his grades cleaned up. I think some are taking a little advantage of that provision for the purpose of getting their grades cleaned up.

There is a very obvious reason why the accredited herd system was devoted to pure bred herds first. It was because of the large number of sales of pure bred animals scattered throughout the Dominion. If any of them had tuberculosis, he would be a much more serious disseminator of the disease than a grade animal that stays at home. If we had abundance of money for this work, I suppose we would be justified in taking up individual grade herds, but I would rather deal with the areas because you get a solid block then. We have nothing like the percentage of infected animals in Canada that they have in Europe or Great Britain. In the first area that we tested, the percentage of reactions was not quite 6 per cent. Then we got it down to one-half of one per cent. Now it is down to one-third of one per cent. In the last area at Huntingdon, in the first test the percentage was between 8 and 9. They have done some of the second test and that shows about 2 per cent of reaction. Consequently, we have not the great difficulty that they have in European countries where sometimes the percentage will amount to three-quarters of the entire number. They are simply throwing up their hands, because they would have to clean out the entire herds. We can pursue a system of eradication without serious loss to or reduction in the herds because of the small number of reactors, though, of course, some herds will be hit seriously.
In the meantime, the problem of the live stock and veterinary world is to find some immunizing vaccine to treat the young calves with and immunize them from disease later on, if possible all through life. Some progress has been made in that respect by what is called the Calmette vaccine, but that immunizes for only from twelve to eighteen months, and only animals not previously affected by tuberculosis. The work is being prosecuted at the labaratory and in isolated herds on the other side of the line. All the veterinary laboratories throughout the world for the last twenty years have been concentrating their activities on getting an immunizing vaccine that can' be used in treating the animals when they are young rather than depending upon eradication by slaughter entirdy. Some of us may live to see this consummated. It may come quite quickly. Some man may be fortunate enough to discover it whom we are not watching at all. Men with great reputations like Calmette, Viallee and Smith and others may be outrun by someone who has not yet been heard of. It is not a matter of luck, but sometimes these things are dropped upon quite 
unexpectedly, and that may occur. But even if that does not occur, the regular men who are looked upon as being in the forefront of this work, are steadily making progress towards the desired end.

I should like to take this
opportunity of replying to the minister's statement that great pressure has been brought to bear upon the government to discontinue this work from certain sections of the country. I know that is a fact. I attended the conference of the Western Live Stock Union at Calgary this year. The deputy minister was also present. I want to pay this tribute to him, that he withstood the attacks of some of those, shall I call them fanatics, from the province of Alberta. I want to congratulate him for undertaking to stand foursquare for this work in face of those attacks. The minister mentioned that he thought the provinces should co-operate with the federal government in connection with this work. He will remember that I have always taken that stand. Although I am from Manitoba, I am quite prepared to go back and take the responsibility for saying that I believe the province of Manitoba should make provision to pay some of the compensation for animals that are slaughtered. We should have the co-operation of the provinces and of the municipalities, and we must have the co-operation of the breeders too if this work is going to be a success. I am convinced that we can eradicate tuberculosis if we go at the work in an aggressive manner. We have succeeded in eradicating glanders and certain other diseases by simply going after them aggressively. I am sorry I am not a veterinary surgeon or I could use those scientific terms. It will take a long time and a good' deal of money to eradicate tuberculosis, but if we roll up our sleeves and put our backs into the work, I believe we can eradicate it also.

I was glad to
hear the minister refer to the little province of Prince Edward Island and say that he thought it would lend itself splendidly to a disease-free area. This matter was brought up last year on this vote, and I pointed out to the minister that we had requests from that province that disease-free areas should be established there. iSince then the matter has been taken up by the Department of Agriculture of that province, and they have sent large petitions, I think, to the department here. I believe the whole province is looking to have it made a disease-free area. As we are not too flush of money down there, I hope it will not be left over until the time

when each of the provinces will have to bear a proportion of the cost, because it would be a great handicap in having the work done. I may say that our province has made splendid progress in dairying and splendid herds have been established there. We have a number of accredited herds, and some of our stock sold exceedingly well. I met a gentleman here a few days !ago from our province who told me that he sold Holstein cows to a farm near here for $1,000. I hope those who have the health of their fellow citizens in this Dominion at heart, as well as the great agricultural and dairying industries of our Dominion, will see that this is a very important work, and that no vote that will ever be presented in this House having this object in view will ever be challenged or in any way interfered with I sincerely trust the minister will give every attention to the request that has come from the province of Prince Edward Island.

Having regard to
the apparent likelihood of the vote going through safely, I feel that I could have a better idea how to lay out next year's work when we get it through council. In addition to that, the area in Quebec has been completed:. It is the first "once over" and we have that off our hands now. I cannot make any hard and fast promises, Mr. Chairman, because after all a certain amount of duty devolves upon the provincial governments in this matter. They have to undertake to prosecute the matter in respect to organizing the campaign, and have to do some compulsory work, where the farmers refuse to have their cattle tested. The Dominion has not the power of compulsion in that regard. We cannot make the statement that we are going to do thus and so when we are co-operating with another government that is to do so and so, before we can go ahead. Two years ago when I was out at the coast I discussed this question with the premier, Hon. John Oliver, and at that time it struck me that the two best areas to conduct these accredited herd operations, because of their natural boundaries, would be Vancouver island and Prince Edward Island, one at one coast
and one at the other. The great trouble with the Carman area was its lack of natural boundaries, and the difficulty of keeping the line of demarcation between what was cleaned up and what was not cleaned up, and travelling back and forth for various reasons; but in the case of Vancouver island or Prince Edward Island, you have a perfect water boundary, and I felt that as soon as the money was available these two areas would be taken up next. I think Prince Edward Island will come first, because this last year or two particularly all the federal members from Prince Edward Island, particularly the hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. MacLean), his colleague from the same riding and the other two members from the province, have been pressing this matter upon me and have assured me that the time is ripe in Prince Edward Island for cleaning up the island and converting it into a Canadian Jersey island. In this island they have practically no T.B. They have one breed of animal and one breed of cow and they have practically no T.B. in the island. Why can we not have a Canadian Jersey island? We cannot hope to have one breed in Prince Edward Island, because there would be a terrific struggle as to which it would be, but there is no reason why we cannot have a Jersey island as far as T.B. is concerned. If we could do this we would have a stimulant, and we could say, "Well, we have one province cleaned up." The same may be said of Vancouver island, but it is a larger area and there is more hinterland, and it would be more expensive to go to the remote points. These are two points we have in mind, and I think everything else being all right and others playing their part in it, there is no reason why we should not take up the matter in Prince Edward Island as soon as possible this summer. That would make one restricted area in the Maritimes, one in the central provinces, one in the prairie provinces and one in British Columbia. That will give us an idea of the probable expense it would be to tackle the country as a whole. We will have some data to place before the municipal and provincial governments as to the cost, as to the percentage of reactors-that is the second and third test-before we would start the campaign. That is the position we are in, and I feel very gratified that the expense is not terrifying us. I may say, however, before we can undertake the campaign in the province of Prince Edward Island we will require to have the wholehearted co-operation of everybody that we have been referring to. They will need to get right behind us.

Replying to the

Mr. Chairman, I do not
claim to be one of the fanatics, -but the Alberta stock men having been referred to as fanatical, I desire to say a word or two on TJ3. testing. In my district hundreds of cows are sent to the block on account of reacting to the tuberculin test. We have cleaned up that district, and we want to be assured that untested cattle will not be sent in there. I have a lot of faith in the efficacy of vaccination to control tuberculosis, but we are not ready to abolish the present system until we know more about the merits of vaccination. These merits have not been proved yet, but I want to commend the government for the research work they are conducting or the benefits that mlay be derived from the adoption of vaccination in place of the present system of T.B. testing. I have been a stock man all my life, and I have always found it better in every way to keep my stock -healthy rather than try to cure them when they became sick. We want to prevent T.B. Like the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader)
I regret the reduced vote, and I would very much dislike to see the work neglected or the present system slackened in any way until we have a better one to take its place, but we have to trust the department. In a dairy district it is perhaps a little more difficult to keep a restricted area clean of tuberculosis because infected cows are being continually weeded out and others are being brought in from outside districts. Therefore I would impress upon the government the necessity of having every animal tested before

it is allowed to be brought into a clean district, and I believe the department is fully alive to the importance of this protective measure. The city authorities of Edmonton are encouraging dairy men to send in milk from tested, healthy cows, and the greater part of the milk used in the city is pasteurized, but some small dairy men are peddling unpasteurized milk. The city authorities want all milk pasteurized in order to guard the people against tubercular infection, and I do not think we can be too careful in this respect. As I understand the new method, the calves should be treated with vaccine just as soon after birth as possible, and before there is time for the disease to develop, because it is thought they do not inherit tuberculosis. Therefore vaccine is used to prevent the cailf taking the disease from the mother's milk or becoming infected in any other way. As I said before, I do not want to be considered fanatical, but I do not feel it is fanatical to encourage the use of vaccine to prevent tuberculosis instead of continuing the present system of T.B. testing indefinitely.

Even with this vote reduced we hope to do just as much work this year as we did last year, not only for the reasons I have indicated but because the work is better organized. In Quebec the percentage was larger than we expected it to be; in Prince Edward Island I am sure the reactors will not be over four or five per cent, perhaps less. In fact, some hon. members from Prince Edward Island have suggested that iit will be as low as two per cent, but I do not hope for that. In any case it will not be as expensive an undertaking as the work in Quebec. We have taken on a good deal more work since the embargo on Canadian cattle was removed. We are obliged by the British law to put a man on every cargo of cattle, and these veterinarians keep the animals under observation all the way across to the Old Country. So that without any addition to the staff we have taken on that new work and are still continuing the old. I assure my hon. friend that the work will not fall back or be neglected; it will be pressed forward and be quite as strong as it was last year. The vaccine to which my hon. friend refers is being tried out on herds in our laboratory over in Hull. Many other discoveries of this nature are placed before the public from time to time; every few weeks the newspaper despatches indicate that somebody has at last found an immunizing vaccine that will prevent the development of tuberculosis in cattle. Two or three weeks ago a despatch appeared in the press to the effect that a very
powerful disinfectant had been discovered at the Johns Hopkins institution at Baltimore which would kill the bug in the animal without destroying the flesh of the animal, something several hundred times stronger than the ordinary disinfectant. Well, that is almost incredible, but there may be something in it. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle has a friend in his riding, a veterinary at Indian Head, who insists that he has a cure not only for bovine tuberculosis, but for tuberculosis in human beings. We would need a stable from here to the Chateau Laurier to test out all these alleged cures, to say nothing of the money required, but we do go as far as we can in that direction. We are doing all that is humanly possible to promote research work, notwithstanding the inadequate facilities we have for it here in Ottawa. There is not a more Slovenly system of departmental buildings in the whole wide world than those used by the Agriculture department right in this capital. We have to make our vaccine in an old house down here on what I will call Slum avenue, between Wellington street and the river, and the research work, so important, is being carried out by Dr. Watson in a laboratory in the house in which he lives. Tnese are not proper conditions and we are trying to correct them. Perhaps we should go faster, but if you knew how I had to sweat to get this much you would feel gratified that it is not less.

I want to thank the minister for the information. I am glad' to bear that he is able to dlo the work just as effectively with less money. There seems to be a fear .in imy part of the country that the present system of tuberculin test will be discarded before the merits of the new method of tuberculin test by use of vaccine, have been proven to be satisfactory. I hope that will not be the case.
Oh no, that will not be done. My hon. friend has heard the old adage "It is best to be off with the old love before you are on with the new." I think that is sound doctrine.

A few nights ago, when we were concluding the discussion on the live stock item, the minister promised that if there were any fag ends of that discussion left over we would have an opportunity of taking them up on this vote. I have had protests from farmers' and stock growers' associations in regard to the rates charged by commission men at the stockyards for handling stock. Has parliament any control over these rates?

Yes. The rates are fixed by the live stock exchanges, but they are submitted to this department for approval. The rate is now $17 per car. That is higher than it used to be, but everything has gone up since the war.

I would like to point out that it was during the war years when the price of cattle went so high that these rates were raised to their present level. Since that time the price of stock has been reduced until now it is not much more than one-third of what it was then, and yet the charges by the commission men on the yards remain just the same as when cattle prices were at their peak. I think it is advisable that some steps be taken to have these charges reduced to something like the former level, or at least that they be brought down very considerably from what they are to-day, for certainly it is not very encouraging to men who are raising live stock to have to pay these high charges on the yards.

We will look into that. The question has been up several times, and the consensus of opinion on the part of those who had to do with the other end and of the officials of the Live Stock branch seems to be that the charge was justified. My recollection is that the pre-war charge was $12.50.
Something like that.

If that is so, the increase is not so excessive as it has been in some other things. I can remember when the rate used to be only $10, but that was a good while ago. However, I will look into it and have the question reviewed.

Are the charges the
same throughout the whole Dominion?
No, they vary with the yards.
Would the minister quote the charges for the various yards?
We have not the record here, although we have a record. The live stock exchanges set the rates, and they are submitted to us for approval.
I thought the minister said his department controlled the rates.

We do. The rates are referred to us in order that we may prevent extortion; but we do not set them. The exchanges set the rate and submit them to us for approval or otherwise. This Live Stock Products Act has only been in force two years now.
The department has the power to reduce rates if they see fit?
We can refuse approval, but I do not think we can impose rates. We can send them back for reconsideration.

Then I would suggest that
they be sent back because at the present time they are much too high compared with the price received for cattle.

I have seen a few
references in the press about the charges, but my recollection is that there has been no serious complaint yet through the ordinary medium. However, I shall look into the whole matter, not only the rates at the western yards but at the eastern yards as well.

Is the minister able to give
me a reply now to the question I asked a few moments ago?
My deputy has not been able to look that up yet, but it is around 150.

The feeling in my district
is that there is a great deal of over-lapping not only in connection with this work but in all the other departments as well. I think if the minister would co-operate with the provincial governments and eliminate this

over-lapping, a reduction in these estimates could be made. I might say further that while the remark made by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie regarding our activities was made in a more or less playtful way, I can assure him that Alberta as a whole is just as sound on this question as any other province. I have a great respect and a great appreciation for a healthy kick if there is anything to kick about, but when there is nothing to kick about, it is about time to

Is it not a fact that The
Western Canada Live Stock Union two years ago at Victoria passed a resolution asking the government to discontinue testing beef
animals?

I think they did
something like that at the tail end of the convention when nearly everyone had gone home or was checking out or something like that. I rather gathered from the
remarks of the minister that the Western Canada Live Stock Union was not very sound, and I was wondering what his definition of the word "sound" was. If "sound" means that you must always agree with the department here, even as to the proper method of testing cattle, of course those men were not "sound." I must admit that I do not know a great deal about this question of testing cattle for tuberculosis, but I do not think that even the minister would deny that they have killed thousands of beef animals as reactors, and after the cattle were slaughtered they could find no sign of disease in the animals.

No, I do not admit anything of the kind It is not a matter of what we think at all. This whole business is entirely voluntary as far as the live stock men are concerned. We do not force them to adopt this plan, we do not even suggest that they should go into it. The merits of the system are what appeal to the live stock men, and they voluntarily come to the government and ask that their herds be brought

under the accredited system. I hope my hon. friend sees the distinction. Far from us forcing or imposing the system on anybody, their entrance into it is entirely and purely voluntary. However, the system possesses such undoubted value to the prospective buyer of live stock, at least dn western Canada thao the live stock men have laid down the condition that before an animal is put up for sale it must be tested and given a certificate of health. This is a regulation adopted by the live stock men themselves and not by the government. I hope my hon. friend the member for Maoleod1 (Mir. Coote) will understand the difference. We are not imposing anything czardike on the people at all. We are very glad to serve them in the matter of T. B., or anything else, if they make the request, that is all.
I must say the minister has just used very different language from what he did a few moments ago when he told of reading the riot act to these poor people.

Well, my goodness! Is my hon .friend as deaf as myself? I was describing what the live stock associations of Manitoba and Saskatchewan did to the live stock union, not what we did. My hon. friend had better get a few more apples on the scene.
Anything for a red herring.

There is no red herring being drawn across the trail here. Go on with your discussion on this question. We will not talk about apples; we will confine ourselves to a discussion on T.B. in cattle as long as my hon. friend likes.
Does the department of hog grading come under this vote?
No.
Does it, or does it not?

No, it does not,
but according to the arrangement the other night we intimated-I think in a moment of weakness-that the live stock question would be discussed under the vote for the Health of Animals branch. My hon. friends took advantage of it the other night in connection with experimental farms. However, we will let the matter go.

Is the minister satisfied with the system followed by his department? I think the object is a very worthy one, but so far as my observation has gone the system is not attaining the end that is sought. We are grading hogs with the idea

of encouraging the farmer to raise a different type of hog, of enabling him to get a higher price for the select bacon type. Now, in the district where I live our hogs are sold to shippers.
Drovers?

Yes. I have inquired
of hundreds of men, but I have never found a single farmer, with one exception, that ever got a cent more for his bacon type hog than he received for his other hogs. The grading is done at the stockyard, and if there is any extra money paid it goes to the drover and not to the farmer. So the department are not succeeding in their efforts to encourage the farmer to raise any different kind of hog. The system is wrong in its application, in some way or other, and I should like to know if there is any probability of its being changed in order to accomplish better results.

I think my hon. friend must have been absent the other night when that subject was discussed very well. However, what I said then will bear repeating possibly. The system is not a perfect one, in which respect it is like the system for combating T.B., but it is an attempt to do something along the line of grading. The correct system is that of grading hogs on the rail, but our country is too large, our abattoirs too far distant, our settlements too widely extended to adopt the plan just as it is followed in Denmark. However, we are trying to do the next best thing, and that is to introduce the principle. This grading is made in two classes-thick smooths and selects. The other grading is a matter of arrangements between the buyer 10 p.m. and seller. The reason the average farmer who sells to the drover does not receive the advantages he should is that the drover buys on a flat rate basis. He does not grade the hogs, he buys them at a flat rate, and if he happens to get any selects among his purchases he is in that much, there is no doubt about that. But the same thing could be said in regard to wheat or any other product, if the farmer refuses to adopt up-to-date methods. In Saskatchewan when I left there they had over 400 live stock shipping associations-I do not remember whether my hon. friend had any in his constituency, I think he had-but there were that number of shipping associations acting in agreement. Under this system the farmers would telephone each other and have a day for shipping. They would bring in their hogs or their cattle, as the case might be, fill up a oar, and send one of their

number down to Winnipeg or wherever the hogs were going. He would attend to all the details and he and his associates would get the benefit of the present system of grading. If the farmer does that he will get the same benefit, but if he sells to a drover he will not get that advantage. As the drover profits in the latter case he discourages the whole idea, and convinces the farmer that there is nothing to the grading system. As long as the farmer sells to the drover he certainly will not get the benefit of the grading. But whenever the farmers get together a carload and send a representative with the car down to Moose Jaw or Winnipeg, or whatever point the hogs are intended for, they will get the benefit of the grade, to the extent sometimes of 10 per cent in the case of selects over the other type. Very little attention was paid to breeding bacon hogs the last few years; especially during the war, a great many of our hogs were of the fat chunky type, not of the bacon type. It is the type of animal which makes bacon that commands the price and meets the competition in the British market. But the department has not been imposing its will on the country. This plan was adopted by the Department of Agriculture, in conjunction with the Hog Breeders' Association in the fall of 1921. My predecessor arranged the plan I believe in this system, and neither the credit, nor the blame if there be any, shoifld be ascribed to me. However I want to associate myself with the men who worked it out. I believe it is a step in the right direction, and that it accomplishes some good for those that it has reached. Those whom the system has not reached do nothing to help themselves; they sell in the old way to the drover. I do not know how we are going to reach those.

The minister said that
the proper place to grade bacon is on the rail. Probably that is where the difficulty lies with respect to hog grading at the present time. The producer of hogs, whether he sells them to a drover and they are sold by that drover to the abattoir, or whether he ships them co-operatively, as was spoken of by the minister, is molt satisfied with the grading as it is at present being carried out. I could tell the minister of a district where the people have .what they believe to be the true bacon type of hog. When this regulation became effective, they got rid of their lard type of hog and purchased the Yorkshire breed of hogs which, I believe, the minister will admit is a bacon type. Shipping co-operatively, however, they are not getting
more than one, two or three per cent of select hogs out of a carload. I believe the producers of hogs in this country are fully alive to the fact that we want to produce a first-class bacon hog if we are going to get the best price in the British market, but the producer when he produces that hog wants to know that he is going to get -fair treatment at the handls of the grader. The only way to do that is not to kick this thing overboard, but to follow it through and to have these hogs graded on the rail as the minister spoke of doing. Our cream is graded into the -creameries and our butter is graded out of the creameries. It seems to me that this matter will not be settled until the same percentage of No. 1 hogs goes into the abattoir and the producer is paid for that as No. 1 bacon goes out. Ilf the minister gave some thought to that phase of the question, he might find a remedy.

The minister said a moment ago that the drovers discourage the farmers as to the grading. There is no need of that, because the farmers are disgusted *with the grading proposition. I live in one of the oldest districts of Manitoba along the Red river where we have improved our hogs according to the instructions igiven by the different authorities on this subject, and we have produced bacon type hogs. But when the grader gets through with them, you do not get any bacon type, you get thick smooth. The farmers to-day are simply disgusted with this grading because they feel that the people who are taking advantage of this grading proposition are either the dealers or the packers. I know in my district the people are not going to raise any more bacon type hogs. They are going to raise thick, smooth hogs because they do not get any grade other than that even if they actually raise the better -grade.

They have the
option of raising any kind they like.

Yes, but no matter how select your hog may be, you are at the mercy of the grader there, and I know of carload after carload of bacon type hogs shipped under the co-operative system where, after the hogs were graded, the producers did not get any selects. All the farmers would get together and one man would take the hogs to the abattoir. It does not take a farmer of extraordinary intelligence to tell whether a hog is bacon type or not. The average farmer who raises hogs can tell, but if you -take the market returns in Winnipeg, you will find that the percentage of selects is very small.

Possibly my hon. friend knows that this matter is going to be discussed before the committee on Agriculture on Tuesday morning and every opportunity will be given to thresh it out. In the meantime, I assume that the objection of my hon. friend and of the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston) is that the hog producers are at 'the mercy of the grader. You have to choose between being at the mercy of the grader and being at the mercy of the packer. Which will you choose? Does the hon. member suggest that the graders are not competent?
It seems so by the way they grade some of the hogs I have seen them grade.

I am afraid that
will bring us back to the Civil Service Commission.
Then abolish the Civil Service Commission.

I do not wish to pass the buck on to them, but in this case I do not think the fault is that of the commission. It is a matter of opinion what constitutes a select bacon hog. There have been very few complaints as regards the character of the graders, and I think they are a capable set of men. The farmers have been accustomed to raising any kind of hog and they do not like not only to have to grade an animal, but to feed at to get it into the select class. Any grading system is objectionable to people whose article is of low quality. If we cannot get into the top grade of wheat, you know how disappointed we are. Remember what disgust there was at the grades of wheat this last fall. Remember what objections were raised to the grading of cream at first. I remember when we started grading in Saskatchewan, many people took their cans out of the creamery and sent their cans down to the Crescent creamery at Winnipeg or Brandon. After a while, they came back. We shall not do our best in the matter of production of hogs or anything else until we realize that in order to get the top price we must have the top grade. If people do not want the top grade or the top money, this is a free country and they can do what they like. In the corn district of western Ontario, they find that it pays them better to raise the fat hog, and they deliberately do that because they are in a com country.

I think the minister has put bis finger on the spot when he says that the right place to grade bacon is on the

rail. It might be that the proper remedy for the trouble is to grade the bacon there and not on foot at all. Is there any record as to the quantity of No. 1 bacon coming out of any particular abattoir in the country?

No, but we have pretty well under way arrangements for grading the bacon. I spoke of it the other night. We have a gentleman over in the Old Country now on the Imperial Marketing committee. When he is through with that, he will go into a further investigation as to the best kind of grades to make to suit the market. It was the first duty to grade the live hog. We cannot grade it on the rail very well in Canada. In Denmark a farmer takes his hogs to the abattoir, goes down town and does his shopping, and in a few hours there is the animal on the rail graded and he gets his money, just as we used to take grist to the mill and in a few hours get the flour back.

A few years ago the country was filled with pamphlets instructing the farmers to raise bacon hogs that would weigh 190 pounds. It was represented' that this made the ideal Wiltshire side and many farmers attempted to produce that kind of hog. Much discontent, however, prevails throughout the country amongst farmers who raise the hogs, the people who handle the co-operative shipments and even the drovers who take the hogs down to the market. There was so much protest made that the department raised the weight of the select bacon hog to 220 pounds.

Two hundred and
ten pounds.

Did this discriminating individual, living in England, advise the minister that it would 'be ail right to raise the weight from 190 to 210 pounds, and if so, why were. the instructions so positive in the first pamphlets that were issued? I do not think the discriminating individual living in England, when he sees his slice of bacon on his plate, can distinguish a difference of five, ten or twenty pounds in a hog. The people are objecting that an individual is required to produce in a bacon type a hog that weighs exactly 210 pounds, but the man on the farm who raises the hog is obliged to put his judgment against the scales in the city of Winnipeg. He has a litter of eight or nine pigs and he guesses at the opportune time to send those pigs to the market. The minister knows full well that a great many people in the west live very many miles from the railway or shipping point, and they
