cannot afford to divide up that litter of hogs; and yet a matter of 4 or 5 pounds of difference in the weight of hogs will penalise that individual $1 per hundred. They will be graded thick smooth, and I think either the cut or the penalty is too great, or the grade is too severe, possibly both. Shortly before I left home I was returning from Winnipeg. Practically all the shippers who live on my line of railway, who go to Winnipeg, were on the train, and the subject of hog grading was the paramount discussion, and naturally it centred around me-what attitude did I take? One old grey whiskered man was in the party and he had had a hard time, but he said "Doc Tolmie is a good old scout. He knows what he is doing". He could not justify the grading but he justified Doc Tolmie. But the people are absolutely dissatisfied with the prices and the system of hog grading and the discrimination shown. I could cite the case of the Watsons-possibly the minister knows of them-living south of Manor, great cattle breeders, who have been on record as having shown cattle at Regina and shipping overseas a number of years. They did secure the type of hogs demanded. I saw a litter of pigs owned by them taken in. I saw them in the yard at Winnipeg and no one could discriminate or see any difference in the hogs by looking at them. I think the scales could scarcely determine the difference. Yet Mr. Watson received one select hog out of the nine, and it was the talk of the whole yard that he was abused, and I really believe it. It is my opinion that unless there is an easing of the principle of grading the people are justified in paying no attention whatever to the grading proposition, or to the attempt to raise that type of hog. If the 190 pound hog was the typical and only hog that would produce the Wiltshire side in 1922, why was it that a year or so afterward we found that a 210 pound hog would make the ideal Wiltshire?

It was in response to the representation made by many farmers. It was a sort, of dividing and harmonizing of interests. The average grower of hogs felt that he could feed hogs to better advantage at 210 pounds, and it was felt it was a sort of compromise, and so it was raised.

Am I right in presuming that if the protest is loud enough there may be another change-that is a change between the select hog and the smooth thick hog, or a discrimination between the hog which weighs 210 pounds and the one which weighs 214 pounds? But the owner of the hog that
is four pounds over is penalized by sacrificing $1 per hundred pounds. I think some of the unrest in this regard could be settled if this discrimination were done away with. A graduated scale such as the minister referred to in the case of wheat might answer the purpose. Let us have a percentage of that, say 25 cents for the hog that weighs five or ten pounds more. A man has to use his judgment by looking at the hog and placing his judgment against the scale weight. He has no control over the. trip to his destination, and by the time the train arrives, his hogs might lose or gain on the trip. It generally takes two days to get a hog down to Winnipeg, depending on the circumstances, but the man who owns the hog pays the full toll and takes all the risk. Therefore I do not think the price should be so discriminatory against the man who is only endeavouring to comply with the regulations with regard to the shipping of the hogs.
Will the minister tell us whether there is any record of the hogs going into the packing plant that get the grade for Wiltshire sides?
No.
No record kept-
There is a record of all the grades, but not of the bacon. We are not grading bacon yet.

If there is a record kept of the number of hogs that get the Wiltshire grade in going into the plant, and the amount of Wiltshire sides sent out of the plant, there is no reason for any quibbling over the grading. We can keep a direct check on it in that way, and I would advise the minister, if it is possible, and as soon as possible to see that there is a record kept of all the hogs that go to the packing plants and get the Wiltshire side grade, and of all the Wiltshire sides going out of the packing plants, that, we may be able to check up and ascertain when the grading is done satisfactorily. I know there is a great deal of dissatisfaction and discouragement. The people who are raising hogs feel that no matter what the quality is they are not getting the Wiltshire grade, when they are entitled to it.	We
want to encourage production of more of the very best quality .possible, and I think that with a small outlay, to keep a check on the hogs that get the Wiltshire grade going into the plant and the amount of Wiltshire pork going out of the plant, we could get at it in a reasonable and intelligent way. and perhaps through the use of this method we will

be able to give encouragement to the people who are trying to raise this kind of hog. It is a very hard thing to do with the breed of hogs we have. It would take some time at the best, but I think that that one thing would give more encouragement than all the talking to the people that the department can do through their agents. Having a check on it and letting the people know they are getting a square deal will help to encourage production.

Referring to the remarks of my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Gould), the grading of hogs in principle is not very much different from the grading of any other product. It is more difficult to carry out, but the principle is the same and you have to have an arbitrary point between grades. The situation is that when you miss one grade and drop into another you drop some money. When you drop a grade in wheat you drop a whole lot-10 or 15 cents between the low grade.
We drop a dollar in one grade on the hog.
That is a cent a pound. That is not as much proportionately as fifteen or twenty cents on wheat. You have to have an arbitrary point of demarcation between one point and another.
Surely a cent a pound on pork is a much greater drop than ten or fifteen cents on 60 pounds of wheat.

That is neither here nor there. You have to have an arbitrary rate. We started out with a weight 160 to 210 pounds. That was changed from 170 to 220 pounds, a sort of compromise. My hon. friend wanted to know whether, if a vigorous kick were made, we would make a change. When you get into the heavier animals you would not have the bacon type. We think we have gone just as far as we can without destroying the grade that is desired abroad. If my hon. friend would just simply imagine that it is something else he is more familiar with-grain-he will acknowledge that you cannot depart from any grading system. This involves exactly what 'he is complaining of. The only way it can be avoided is by having a straight sample market where one man dickers with another. Once you begin to grade, you must have an arbitrary line, and the moment you drop out of one grade into the lower you drop money. If it only made 5 per cent difference it would take an expert to tell it. Besides, nobody but the buyer sets the price; the market says what the grade

will bring, not the grader. The packer comes along and is ready to give 10 per cent more for that kind of animal. You wonder why he will not give more, but that is what it is worth to him who is converting the raw product into the finished article to compete with other countries. Let me read the description of select bacon hogs:
Select bacon: hogs weighing 170 to 220 pounds at stockyards and abattoirs, or hogs weighing 170 to 220 pounds at local shipping points and at such other points as may be designated from time to time; of a type and finish indicating suitability for the production of choice bacon or Wiltshire sides for export. Jowl and shoulder light and smooth; back from neck to tail evenly fleshed; side long, medium depth, dropping reasonably straight from back; ham full; good general finish; no excess fat.
It takes a bird of a hog to comply with that description. You might have a heavy shoulder and heavy neck animal with short side and fat hams; that would not do at all. The owner of any product is always a little partial towards it just as we are partial to our own children. Therefore it would not be safe to leave the grading to the owner; it has to be done by some impartial individual, and it takes an expert. These graders become so familiar with their work that although the animals pass by them quickly their judgment is very seldom challenged. I have been well pleased with any of these graders whom I have seen at work. I know the difficulty I had in converting myself from the old-fashioned idea I got when a youth down in this province. We used to think a hog was not ready for the knife until it was so fat that you had to call it three or four times before it would get up. Some education is needed to get that idea out of a man in favour of something that looks to him more like a greyhound-a thin, smooth animal, with long sides-where the value is-and low shoulders 

where the low price is-and a light neck. I am afraid a great many farmers are setting up the judgment of their youth against the new demand; they .want to make the grade fit their hog, instead of making their hog fit the grade. I had the same difficulty myself, and it is only in the last ten years that I have paid much attention to the matter at all. I am in correspondence with the provincial ministers of agriculture, on this very thing, asking them if they have any suggestions to make to improve conditions-Do they agree with the principle? If so, what details should be changed to make it more acceptable to the farmer? If anybody does not want to comply with the grading, well, this is a free country and he can grow anything from a wild boar to a razorback, but if he wants to get the price he must raise select bacon hogs.

he thought it possible to keep a record of the hogs going into the plant getting the Wiltshire side grade and the pork going out of the plant.

I overlooked that
question. When we come to grade the bacon, yes; but at present the grading does not go past the live hog. We are working on the system of bacon grading now. In a few months we hope to have it ready, and then we will have, a check on the amount that goes in and the amount that comes out. But make no mistake, when we put that on there will have to be a few more men, and this increase of staff will bring a few more complaints from some people that we are blowing in too much money for the work. It must be understood that if we are going to give service we must pay the price.

It is not satisfactory at
the present time, so I am glad to hear the minister is going to see the work will be done in a better way.

It is a gradual
evolution towards betterment.

When on my feet before I
do not think I said anything which should cause the minister to think that I object to the principle of grading.

I do not think
you did.

I do not object to the principle of grading although I notice it is very fashionable at the present time to grade the farmers' stuff as it leaves him, but it is not as fashionable to grade the stuff which the farmer has to buy. I should like to see the same activity and persistence in the other departments of the government to grade the materials which I have to buy as is shown in the grading of materials which I have to sell. The minister read to the committee the type of hog which makes the Wiltshire sides, and one of the items was "not much fat."
No excess fat.

Not enough fat to put in
your lard pail at all.
Mr, MOTHERWELL:	Very little.

The market has been stolen by the Cottolene people, the people whom the minister two years ago scolded so severely because of their product entering into the manufacture of oleomargarine, but he has handed over the shortening market to these same people.
There will always be enough fat hogs to produce lard.

Possibly, but at the present
time I notice the lard pails are particularly low, and I have to go into the butcher shop to buy cottolene or crisco, which have taken the place of the real, genuine old lard that helped to make the genuine old doughnuts "like mother used to make," and which now are denied us through the activities of the Department of Agriculture.

We will have to
get oleo back then to make doughnuts.

The minister must recognize how difficult it is for the farmer taking the chance on his own judgment to get his hogs to the Winnipeg market and have them come within this narrow margin of weight. It may be a true type that was bred properly and ordinarily would have conformed to the weight requirement had the facilities for getting to market been as they should be. But something happened; the hog was longer on the road than it should have been, or it may have been fed, with the result that it weighed a pound more than it should have weighed and the owner loses one cent a pound on that account. There is an argument in favour of the man who has made an honest attempt to turn out the proper type of hog. The people in my part of the country are dissatisfied with the principle of hog grading as it is now carried out.
My hon. friend approves, I understand, of the principle of grading. What changes would he suggest in detail?

I would be as broad in
my interpretation of what the change should be as the minister was when he raised the weight from 190 to 210 pounds. If license was shown to that extent when that change was made, then I think a further license might be shown in determining what the weight and the status of the bacon hog should be at the present time.
The market has to set the price.

I do suggest the advisability of grading bacon out. I believe that the abattoirs or storage houses that check in these supposed thick smooths and bacon hogs are sending out more Wiltshire sides than they take in. I think it is the business of the government to know that and to see that the people are informed generally of the condition of affairs in that regard.

Supply-Agriculture

This matter of hog grading is one in which everyone is interested. I am sorry to hear from the hon. member (Mr. Gould) that there is a shortage in the doughnut crop as the result of the grading regulations; but it appears to be largely a matter of education. We cannot hope to consume all the hogs that we grow in this country and we cannot hope to market them in those markets that are open to us in the face of the competition from other countries unless we produce the kind of bacon they want. It is easier to do that than to change their ideas of what they want. I would like to commend the minister for the work he is carrying on in his agricultural committee in connection with the giving of addresses by experts of the department. I understand there is to be an address on the bacon hog and hog grading next week.
Tuesday.

Why not follow that up with a live hog demonstration, either at the packing house over in Hull or at the experimental farm, so that all the mesmfoeiB of the House of Commons who take a keen interest in .this matter may have the opportunity to see an actual demonstration of what the bacon hog is?
I shall be very glad to do that.

There has been so much criticism of hog grading and the types of grades set out by the department that I cannot help thinking that a little support should be given to the system or to the grades as at present established, by one who feels that he knows what he is talking about. I happen to have been connected with this hog grading work-
Does the hon. member suggest that those who spoke against the grades did not know what they were talking about?

Not at all, but I claim that I know what I am talking about when I support .the grades that have been established.
I was interested in the agitation for the grading of hogs for some years before it was adopted and in several conferences with representatives of the packing plants of Ontario. We have demonstrated at our local shipping point at home that the farm there is receiving a benefit from the system, because os a result of it, we are getting a premium ranging from $40 to $70 on every week's shipment.

What percentage
goes "select?"
IMr. Gould.]

It varies. When we first started to grade, our loads ranged from 12 to 15 per cent-12 was the lowest. We have gained from 12 per cent to 58, to my knowledge, and it may have increased within the last week or two. We have done that in a matter of eight or nine months. It is not hard to prodhlce a hog that will Comply with the grades laid down by the department. Care has to be taken, in the breeding, and particularly in the feeding in the early months of the life of .the hog. It is when the hog is young that the hog is made. You cannot raise hogs in Ontario to-day by letting them grow themselves; they have to foe grown just the same as any other animal.

Do you dairy as
well?

Yes. You cannot profitably raise hogs without keeping milch cows. I hope that the campaign of hog grading will continue to the point that different hon. members have suggested, and that we will have an actual check or report on the bacon as it leaves the plant. I understand that we are allowing a great deal of American bacon to be .brought into Canada, cured here 'and sold in Great Britain. I have tried to get a copy of the mark that is stamped on the bacon but I am told that the words "Canadian cured" appear in rather large letters and "American bacon" in small letters, and that the bacon is frequently sold in Great Britain as Canadian bacon. If we are to spend a great deal of money and time ito establish our reputation as a bacon producing country we should have our markets very closely watched to see that no one else cuts in on us. I would like to be certain that this American bacon is not injuring the reputation of our Canadian bacon in Great Britain.

There was a general impression that during the war the reputation of our bacon was injured a little by the American bacon that my hon. friend speaks about; and we may have hurt it a little ourselves during that period. A very large amount of this bacon comes in-about 25,000,000 pounds a year. That is brought into the packing houses. It is kept separate and put into separate vats. It is cured separately, and shipped out separately. It is one of the duties of the meat inspector to see that it is shipped out separately and marked separately, every side being marked " U.S. product." I do not think there is any abuse now. The only thing that I have felt anxious about was this:	When Canadian packers

Supply-Agriculture
could not get the amount of Canadian bacon wanted, instead1 of pressing for it and by offering a fair price encouraging the Canadian farmer, they turned around and bought from the United States in order to keep their plant going. You cannot blame them for that; but if that were not done, they would be more likely to pay a better price and encourage bacon production here. The idea is to make it so attractive that they could not afford to miss it. If I were a packer, I presume I would want to keep my plantrunning at full capacity, and the only way for us to stop them importing is to raise more bacon. I know fanners do not like anybody suggesting anything to them about hogs, because they feel they have been fooled on hogs so often they want to be left alone; but you cannot blame the packer for importing if he cannot get enough at home to keep his plant running.

I think it would be
wise for our customs officials or for the department to see that the words " Canada " and " Canadian " are not allowed to go on the packages or on American meat shipped in here.

Those words are
not allowed.

Not even "Canadian
cured." Do not let the words Canada or Canadian appear on it at all.

I have heard it
stated that " Canadian -cured " is on it, but I am sure it is not.

To return to the item before us, I am quite sure the minister in his zeal for economy would welcome any suggestion which, if feasible, would assist him in reducing the cost of administration of this and similar acts without impairing the efficiency of the service. In answer to a question by the hon. member for Victoria, the minister stated there was no over-lapping of the work of the veterinaries employed in this department and those who might be employed by provincial departments. I want to suggest to him that it might be possible in a great many cases to use some of the local veterinaries for that work. We have a considerable staff of men employed in this business, and not only are they on salary but they also have to travel long distances, at considerable expense, to reach the scene of their operations. I believe,-as a matter of fact I know from personal observation that there are a great many local veterinaries in the neighbourhood, competent men who for 5&i
a comparatively small fee would perform that work. I believe that is a suggestion that is worth considering. I -have heard it stated, not only by the local veterinaries but by farmers in the neighbourhood-and I have myself seen it-that men have travelled upwards of one hundred miles by train and by car to do that work, at great expense for travelling and involving a loss of time, which means that they can do comparatively little work. I would like the minister to consider that suggestion.
I think the same principle -might be applied in connection with some of the other acts; for instance the Live Stock Act; I would not have referred to that if it had not been mentioned here to-night. There are three or four items; take these stallion clubs, for example. I understand that in order to qualify, a horse must be subjected to an inspection by a qualified horseman in order to ascertain whether the animal is of. the proper type. I had a very interesting experience in -the city of Calgary not very long ago. I was in the Pa-lliser hotel and saw there a gentleman very comfortably ensconced. I said to one of my friends. "Do you know who that man is?" "Yes," he said "he is a horseman from Ontario. He has come up to inspect stallions for stallion clubs." " What is the idea?" I asked. "Oh," he said "we haven't good enough horsemen in Alberta to do the work, I presume." I want to suggest to the minister that in many cases you will find! in Alberta, not in the same -district, for it is not always advisable to use 'a man in the same district, but in the neighbourhood horsemen as well qualified to do this work as any horseman anywhere else in Canada. They would be -glad to do it for a comparatively small fee for each examination. If that can be done, and of course I am prepared to listen with an open mind to any reasons why it cannot be done, I am quite certain it would! result in a considerable reduction in staff, and a consequent decrease in salary and travelling expenses and result in the case of examination of horses in a great reduction of fees and expenses charged by the men who do the inspection. I have men in my own district who I know are just as well qualified to pass on the pedigree and type of horse required as any man imported to do the work. They could examine a horse for $10, whereas I am sure my friend in the Palliser hotel would have charged at least $100 in fees and expenses to do the same work. I would like the minister to consider that, and ascertain if some system of that sort could not be put -into force in connection with many
Supply-A gricul ture

of these acts. We have ,a great many grading acts now, and we will probably have more. I am not against grading acts; I would like to see the grading acts lived up to and our products standardized and improved and the health of every animal maintained, and we should have competent men to see they are maintained; but I would suggest that as we are continually multiplying these services, which means a continual increase in the staff employed, and a continual increase in expenditure, some such system as I suggest might in many cases be put into force. It would materially reduce the cost without impairing in any way the efficiency of the work done; I would be very sorry to see its efficiency in any way impaired.

I think the remarks of my hon. friend are worthy of some notice. His suggestions look quite plausible, but we have found in actual practice that it is better to have an outside examiner of these horses, just as it is better to have outside judges at fairs on account of the keen competition there is among the stock men. An outside examiner will be more likely to give a fair (and unbiased examination, other things being equal, than the local man who is influenced by his home environment and associations, and may be persuaded into giving not quite as fair a judgment on the merits of the animal.

I was not suggesting
that a man in the district in which the club was formed should do that work. I am quite aware that local circumstances might influence his judgment, but a man could be brought in from a district not so very far away to do it.

That often happens, I believe. In the instance my hon. friend mentions, the man might have come from Ontario, but we have no desire to pay heavy travelling expenses if we can get a good man locally.
My hon. friend's other point about local veterinaries also sounds plausible, but our certificate, whether it is on our meats or any other product, and with regard to freedom from tuberculosis, our inspection certificates of all kinds in order to have value must be given by our own men. I think that is a condition in other countries also. It must be men under the control and in the pay of the federal government. Our certificate would have very little weight unless it was given by our own men; in fact we have to comply with the conditions laid down by other countries in this respect. If those

countries want their bacon certified it must be marked by a federal veterinary. If the market wants our cattle to be certified free from T.B. that certification must be done by an appointee of the federal government. We do not create these terms, other countries insist on them, and it is our duty to comply with these demands just as it is in the matter of sending a veterinary over to the Old Country with every consignment of cattle. Under these conditions, therefore, we are not permitted to use the services of local men, particularly in the case of exportations to the overseas market. As to the men who are employed by the federal department I- must refer hon. gentlemen to the Hunter building-that is the place where the positions go through. We have not advertised for any veterinaries recently; there is a waiting list of about forty or more of men who have qualified. There may be some men from Alberta, I think there are some from Saskatchewan, on that list, but the general understanding is that appointments from this list will be made on the basis of eligibility. Not only that, but the order with regard to certificates precludes the possibility of appointing local men.

I think the minister is mistaken in his conception of my suggestion in one respect. I am not objecting to veterinaries being appointed from other provinces and stationed permanently in Alberta, I am not objecting because they are not Alberta vets, but I was suggesting that it might be possible to have these men examined by the federal department and placed, if you like, on part time, as is done in many departments of the government.
Yes, we do that.
These part time men would be remunerated on the fee system, but would still be federal employees who would comply with the provisions of the act.
We have that system now.
I was suggesting you should extend that system and pay these men on a per diem basis.

I wish to say one or two words in connection with the vote under consideration. The minister, with reference to the creation of isolation areas for the purpose of cleaning up tuberculosis, referred to Vancouver island and also to Prince Edward Island. The suggestion is a very excellent ODe for the reason the minister stated-that in both cases there are natural barriers, the areas can be easily isolated, and the needed isolation

Supply-Agriculture
can be maintained to the greatest possible extent. On Vancouver island a great deal of testing has already been done under the provincial government. There are a number of accredited herds there, and in addition to that we have perhaps one of the best Jersey herds and Jersey equipments in the whole of Canada. So that the department when it undertakes that work, will find the conditions very good to begin with.
The minister has spoken about the provincial aid that his department should receive in carrying on the work of the Health of Animals branch. While I quite agree that that aid would be an advantage, we must guard carefully what has been built up in connection with that branch. It stands out by itself as one of the best organizations of its kind in the world, created largely on a splendid foundation laid by the late Dr. J. G. Rutherford, a man whom we all respected, and whom we all acknowledge to have been, perhaps, one of the ablest men in his profession in the country. We have attained a position that is unique from the point of view of the success that has been achieved. Perhaps the strongest arguments that were used before the embargo commission in the Old Country were first our freedom from animal contagious disease, and, in the second place, our ability to continue to protect the herds erf Canada against contagious disease. iSoi that in any arrangement that is made with any province I would advise the careful guarding of the authority of the federal Health of Animals branch in order that that authority may remain unimpaired. That branch has succeeded in the past, it is succeeding at the .present time, and gives every promise of being able to succeed in the future.
There is a point I should like to refer to for a moment, and that is the cutting down of the amount of compensation paid. The compensation, as I understand it, is a means of paying to the man who is losing the diseased cattle a certain amount of remuneration so as to diminish his loss. We found at the beginning that all this health of animals work was opposed, just as hog grading is being opposed to-day, but when people began to realize the value of the work a fair compensation was a tremendous aid1 to the government in carrying on its operations. It is rather dangerous to lower your compensation too much. In the case of the small farmer who has a small grade herd, after he has raised his steer and his heifer to the yearling stage I do not see just what difference it will make. The value of both animals is practically the same whether
yearlings or two year olds; and I think he should have compensation coming to him just as much in the one case as in the other; I am quite sure that he suffered a loss in both cases.
It has been mentioned to-night in the discussion that there was somewhat of an inclination to get away from the splendid work carried on by the Health of Animals branch at one of the meetings in the west during the past year. If that be so I think that tendency should be very strongly opposed. We find in all districts, and I have had a personal experience in this connection, that in applying the regulations of the Health of Animals branch there is always a group that will oppose you strongly under all conditions; and you simply have to go after them with a stiff upper lip and put the regulations through. If the regulations are properly applied the opponents will, in the course of time, come to recognize the value of them.
There is one criticism I am going to make -although I am not going to say it is the only one I should like to offer-and that is of the policy of spending large amounts
11 p.m. of money on compensation while there is only a very small sum expended on research work. It appears to me that research work-good and extensive research work-should be the foundation of the entire operations of the Health of Animals branch to a very great extent, and that by carrying on this research work, by learning the very best method of conducting experiments with the proper plant, you will place yourself in a position, after a while, to avoid a great deal of the expenditure that is now made in the way of compensation. I would strongly urge upon the government that these stations be extended so as to afford the experts that you have at the present time, and very excellent men they are, a fair opportunity of developing along these lines, remembering that trying to economize will not make the germs inactive; they will continue to keep busy under all circumstances, and so there must be adequate appropriations to carry on the work in a proper way.
Before closing I should like to ask the minister one question:	Did I understand him to
say, when discussing the Calmette vaccine that this has not reached a sufficiently high standard of perfection to be adopted as a general method of eradicating tuberculosis?

We are experimenting, but we could not, as yet, recommend any general application.
Supply-A griculture

From the knowledge you
have acquired, and in the opinion of your experts, it has not yet reached that stage?
That is right.

What amount of money is
being spent in research work with the object of preventing or stamping out these diseases?
I think I read the item out. "Pathological division, $55,000."

I ask the minister why
he has undertaken to exempt cattle suffering fronj. lump jaw from any -compensation if they react to the tuberculin test? I, as a breeder and live stock man do not take any serious objection to the fact that this is applied to Steers. But for the life of me I cannot, see why they apply this to cattle suffering from lump jaw. I took occasion to write to the Veterinary Inspector General to see if there was any connection between lump jaw and tuberculosis. One clause in his letter reads:
The whole trouble with lump jaw is that the cases are not promptly dealt with. In cases that are promptly dealt with and recover, there is no sign of any enlargement. This disease has no bearing at all upon tuberculosis.
If a breeder is unfortunate enough to have a very valuable female animal contract lump jaw, she gets over it, she has had no tuberculosis and there is no scar left from her having had lump jaw, why should the breeder of that animal be penalized to the extent that he will not get compensation for her if she reacts to the tuberculin test? The regulations call for her destruction, but there is no compensation. Why is that regulation in effect?

When this disease
is in its incipient stage and can be taken care of, I think the intention is not to apply the regulation to that stage; but when the disease gets so far advanced, objectionable and repulsive that the animal should not be there at all, we want the regulation to apply to that. In the early stages we can give compensation.
I want that clearly brought out. In the incipient stage where there are no sufficient signs, compensation would not be withheld in case of a reaction?
No.

Has the minister control over insurance rates charged by live stock commission agents? They Charge an insurance rate on each car, the premium running from eight to ten, to twelve dollars a car, to protect them against probable losses from

animals that may fail to pass the test. Many complaints are made by farmers and drovers that a very much larger -amount is paid in than the actual value of the losses. There are hundreds of cars on which I am assured there are no losses at all, and yet this amount of eight, ten or twelve dollars is paid on every one of them. Those -men should be compelled to -furnish a statement -showing their actual losses and the value as against the amount that they collect in insurance premiums.

That is a pretty old question to open up at this time of the evening. I think the principle of charging a flat rate for insurance to take care of disease is bad, because it is charging the man with the clean stock just the same as the man with dirty stock. But in the absence of any better system, the packers have been carrying this on for quite a long time. This question has been raised, as the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie) knows, at practically every live stock meeting that has been held for the last ten or twelve years and at every live stock union that has been held.

The complaints I have heard in this regard are not because the men with the clean stock have to pay the same as those with the poor grade stock, but that a much larger amount is paid in than the packers actually lose. My suggestion is that these commission agents should be compelled to furnish statements showing the value of their actual losses as against the amounts they collect, because I believe they make a good deal of money out of those premiums.

Item agreed to.
Entomology, $20,000.
We have had a pretty busy night; this is the end of the week, and most of our people have gone away. I think we have done pretty well.
This is Friday and tomorrow is a holiday. We might go on for another hour.

That is not reasonable.
We have bad an excellent discussion to-day just as we had on the previous item. The minister has carried three very large items running into about $5,000,000 besides some smaller items. I think he ought to be well satisfied with the day's work.
Progress reported.
On motion of -Mr. Beland the House adjourned at 11.10 pun.
